INTERPRETATION OF STATUTES — legislative intent, case law and parliamentary debates as aids to interpretation — principles of interpretation applied to human rights legislation from other statutes — plain meaning rule — context — constitutional remedies applied to human rights legislation — HUMAN RIGHTS — principles used to interpret Charter applied to human rights legislation — human rights legislation subject to other enactments — nature and purpose of human rights legislation — enforcement of rights — sexual orientation as an analogous ground of discrimination under the Charter — APPEALS AND JUDICIAL REVIEW — error of law in interpreting legislation

EQUALITY — relationship between equality under human rights legislation and equality under the Charter — equality in the administration, substance and benefit of the law —
CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS
—
s. 15(1)
(equality) — application of
s. 1
(reasonable limits) and application of Oakes test — s. 32 (application of Charter) — SEXUAL ORIENTATION — sexual orientation as ground of discrimination in human rights legislation — definition of sex discrimination includes sexual orientation — DISCRIMINATION — protection based on non-enumerated grounds of discrimination

CONSTITUTIONAL LAW — constitutional remedies of reading in, striking down, and striking down or severance and temporarily suspending declaration in invalidity — FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS — Constitutional guarantees as limits to rights provided in provincial legislation — REMEDIES — constitutional remedies — COURTS — authority of court to order constitutional remedy — EVIDENCE — judicial notice

Summary:
This is an appeal by Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Alberta from a decision of the Court of Queen's Bench which ruled that
ss. 2(1)
,
3
,
4
,
7(1)
and
10
of the
Individual's Rights Protection Act
(IRPA) infringe
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter of Rights
and Freedoms because of their failure to include and enumerate sexual orientation as a prohibited ground of discrimination. The Court of Queen's Bench ordered that sexual orientation be read into the IRPA.

In a split two-one decision, the Alberta Court of Appeal overturns this decision, ruling that the omission of sexual orientation from the list of prohibited grounds of discrimination in the
IRPA
does not constitute an infringement of
s. 15
.

This action was commenced by Delwin Vriend who was hired as a laboratory co-ordinator by King's College in Edmonton in December 1987, and fired in January 1991 when the College learned that Mr. Vriend is gay. Mr. Vriend made a complaint to the Alberta Human Rights Commission alleging that he was discriminated against with respect to employment because of his sexual orientation. His complaint was rejected because the
IRPA
does not prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation. Mr. Vriend then commenced an action under
s. 15
of the
Charter
, claiming that the IRPA violates
s. 15
because it does not provide protection from discrimination based on sexual orientation.

The Supreme Court of Canada issued its decision in Egan v. Canada prior to the completion of this appeal, ruling that homosexuals are a group entitled to the protection of s. 15. Consequently, the three outstanding issues in this appeal are:

(1) Does the omission of sexual orientation from the
IRPA
violate
s. 15
?

(2) If so, can the violation be justified under
s. 1
of the
Charter
?

(3) If not, what is the appropriate remedy?

The Alberta Court of Appeal issues three separate judgments.

McClung J.A. finds that there is no governmental action involved here to which
s. 15
of the
Charter
can apply. The Legislature has not acted; rather, when it did not include sexual orientation in the prohibited grounds in the
IRPA
, it declined to act. Legislative inactivity is not law.

In addition, McClung J.A. finds that the
IRPA
is neutral; it makes no distinction between homosexuals and heterosexuals. In fact, it extends full protection to heterosexuals and homosexuals alike who may be discriminated against on the grounds presently specified. In its current state, the IRPA leaves heterosexuals the choice of contracting with, or employing, homosexuals. It does not force them to do so. Similarly, homosexuals may choose to contract with heterosexuals, or not. There is nothing in the record to prove that any discrimination will result.

Governments do not have to emulate the
Charter of Rights
and Freedoms in their legislative responses to human rights. There is considerable variation across the country in the prohibited grounds included in human rights acts, and latitude must be allowed to local lawmakers, especially provinces, to implement their powers under s. 92 of the Constitution Act.

Finally, McClung J.A. finds that judges should exercise self-restraint, and not mechanically invade the legislative area because human rights are involved.

McClung J.A. rules that there is no s. 15 violation, and concludes that it is not necessary to address s. 1 extensively. However, McClung J.A. finds that the response of the Alberta Legislature reasonably balances competing social demands which our society must address. He is unable to conclude "that it was a forbidden, let alone a reversible, legislative response for the Province of Alberta to step back from the validation of homosexual relations, including sodomy, as a protected and fundamental right, thereby ”˜rebutting a millennia of moral teaching'..."

Although it is not necessary to his judgment, on the question of remedy, McClung J.A. finds that the Court of Queen's Bench erred in ordering that sexual orientation be read in. The preferable response in a case of this kind, if a violation were found, would be a declaration of invalidity, with a stay, in order to allow a grace period for the Legislature to repair the legislation.

In a concurring judgment, O'Leary J.A. finds that the
IRPA
does not create a distinction based on sexual orientation. Though in some circumstances a statute may infringe s. 15 by what it fails to say, in the present case the IRPA makes no distinction whatsoever between heterosexuals and homosexuals, or between any individuals or groups on the basis of sexual orientation. The circumstances here are not analogous to those in the case of Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, for example, where the challenged legislation expressly extended the eligibility to practice law in B.C. to all citizens, but, by limiting it to citizens excluded non-citizens from that benefit. To be analogous, the IRPA would have to extend some benefit to heterosexuals which it denies to homosexuals. That is not the case here. The statute is silent on the matter of sexual orientation. Consequently, it does not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation.

O'Leary J.A. also finds that s. 15 should not be read to require legislatures, if they enter into the field of human rights legislation at all, to extend protection and benefits to the same extent as
s. 15
of the
Charter
. Section 15 of the Charter does not require human rights legislation to place all disadvantaged individuals and groups on an identical footing. Section 15 inquiries must be directed at whether a law distinguishes in a discriminatory manner on the basis of a prohibited or analogous ground, not whether the law fails to provide protection against every enumerated and analogous ground of discrimination.

In the present case, any distinction between the way that homosexuals and heterosexuals are treated is not due to the
IRPA
, but rather exists independently of the legislation. O'Leary J.A. concludes that there is no violation of
s. 15
of the
Charter
.

In dissent, Hunt J.A. examines the recent decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada in Miron v. Trudel, Egan v. Canada, and Thibaudeau v. Canada. She finds that it is not clear that currently there is a majority view on the Supreme Court about the meaning of "discrimination" in s. 15. Rather, there are three different approaches.

The first approach, followed by McLachlin, Cory, Iacobucci and (probably) Sopinka JJ. requires a two-step s. 15 analysis. The questions asked in these steps are:

(1) Has there been a denial of one of the four equality rights (equality before the law, equality under the law, equal benefit of the law, equal protection of the law) due to a distinction created by the impugned law? Has the challenged law drawn a distinction between the claimant and others, based on personal characteristics?

(2) Does the distinction constitute discrimination? To show discrimination, it must be shown that the denial of equality rests upon an enumerated or analogous ground, and that "the unequal treatment is based on the stereotypical application of presumed group or personal characteristics?"

The second approach followed by Gonthier, La Forest, Major JJ. and Lamer C.J. has three steps. They are:

(1) Has the law drawn a distinction between the claimant and others?

(2) Does the distinction result in disadvantage; does the impugned law impose a burden, obligation or disadvantage on a group to which the claimant belongs that it does not impose on others?

(3) Is the distinction based upon an irrelevant personal characteristic protected by s. 15? What is the personal characteristic; and is it relevant to the functional values underlying the legislation? Discrimination under s. 15 may be rebutted by a finding that the ground on which the equal treatment is denied is relevant to the legislative goals or functional values underlying the impugned law.

The McLachlin group takes issue with this approach, finding that even if the distinction is relevant, it is necessary to go on to examine the effect of the distinction in the social and economic context of the legislation and the lives of the individuals it touches. If the functional values underlying the legislation are defined in terms of the alleged discriminatory ground, the basis of the distinction will necessarily be relevant to the legislative aim. The reasoning can become circular, unless the impact of the distinction on the members of the targeted group is examined.

The third approach, followed by L'Heureux-Dubé J., focuses on the purpose of s. 15, which is to recognize each person's equal worth as a human being, regardless of individual differences. A person or group is discriminated against under s. 15 when members of the group have been made to feel, by virtue of the impugned legislative distinction, that they are less worthy of recognition as human beings. This definition focuses on impact, that is, the discriminatory effect, rather than on the grounds of the distinction.

Following this approach, a claimant must show that there is a legislative distinction; that it results in a denial of one of the four equality rights; and that the distinction is discriminatory. A distinction is discriminatory where it is capable of promoting or perpetuating the view that the individual adversely affected is less capable, or less worthy of recognition or value.

In the view of L'Heureux-Dubé, the "relevance" approach is untenable, because it fails to take into account the possibility that a distinction that is relevant to the purpose of the legislation may nonetheless have a discriminatory effect.

Hunt J.A. finds that all three approaches require that under s. 15 there must be a distinction that gives rise to interference with one of the four equality rights, and the distinction must be discriminatory. The differences arise over the meaning of "discrimination." La Forest and Gonthier JJ. indicate that if the distinction is relevant to the legislative goals, there will be no discrimination, unless those goals themselves can be said to offend
Charter
values. But McLachlin, Cory and Iacobucci JJ. indicate that a distinction that is relevant to the legislative goals may still be discriminatory, if it impacts upon the claimant in a way that is contrary to the purpose of s. 15, namely, if the distinction stereotypes rather than evaluates based upon individual merit.

Hunt J.A. considers that this case presents an issue that has not yet been decided by the Supreme Court of Canada. The
IRPA
offers protection to certain groups that have been the victims of discrimination; it does not offer the same protection to homosexuals, who have also been the victims of discrimination. Does the legislative silence or omission amount to the drawing of a distinction?

Hunt J.A. concludes that there are various ways to approach this question. However, she finds that legislatures cannot avoid s. 15 merely by failing to extend a protection or benefit to a particular group. A failure to legislate can of itself attract
Charter
scrutiny. Whether that failure to act will run afoul of the Charter will depend on whether the purpose of the Legislature in failing to act is to encourage or support the distinction between groups that are protected and those that are not.

In this case, given the facts found by the trial judge, Hunt J.A. finds that the purpose of the Legislature's failure to protect homosexuals under the
IRPA
is to encourage and support the distinction between homosexuals and other victims of discrimination who are protected. In this case, the failure to extend protection to homosexuals under the IRPA can be seen as a form of government action that is tantamount to approving ongoing discrimination against homosexuals. The purpose of the Legislature's refusal to act is to reinforce stereotypical attitudes about homosexuals and their individual worth and dignity. This is a case where legislative silence draws a distinction.

Hunt J.A. rejects the argument that the
IRPA
is neutral and treats Vriend in the same way as others. This is to ignore the most fundamental element of the case: it is as a result of his homosexuality, an analogous ground under
s. 15
of the
Charter
, that he is being treated differently.

Considering the question of whether the distinction is discriminatory, Hunt J.A. finds that whether one takes the McLachlin, Cory, Iacobucci JJ. approach, or the Gonthier, La Forest JJ. approach, one must conclude that there is discrimination. Taking the McLachlin approach, it is clear that Vriend is being denied equal protection and benefit of the law not because of his merit or his need but purely because of his homosexuality. He was fired not because of his abilities, but because of presumed characteristics attributed to him because of his homosexuality. Denial of access to the
IRPA
reinforces the stereotype that homosexuals are less deserving of protection and therefore less worthy of value as human beings.

Taking the Gonthier approach, one must conclude that the functional values of the
IRPA
are articulated in the preamble which refers to the "inherent dignity of all persons." It is impossible to see how a statute based on notions of the inherent dignity of all can have as a relevant legislative goal the unequal treatment of some members of society as regards employment. Thus, this is a case where the functional values underlying the omission of homosexuals are themselves discriminatory.

Hunt J.A. concludes that in this case a distinction has been drawn between homosexuals and other victims of discrimination through the Alberta Legislature's refusal to make homosexuality a prohibited ground of discrimination. As a result, Delwin Vriend has been denied equal benefit and protection of the law. This distinction is discriminatory.

Turning to
s. 1
of the
Charter
, Hunt J.A. finds that there is no evidence that denying human rights protection to homosexuals is a legislative objective that is pressing and substantial. The fact that the protection is controversial does not make the denial of it a pressing concern. Many other human rights protections have been controversial in their time.

Also, the denial of protection is not rationally connected to the purpose of the legislation. The purpose of the legislation is to extend protection to groups that have historically been disadvantaged; the omission of sexual orientation has the opposite effect. Nor does the impugned provision minimally impair the
Charter
right. The exclusion from protection is total, so there is a total impairment of the Charter guarantee of equality. Hunt J.A. concludes that the denial of protection is not a reasonable limit under s. 1.

Finally, Hunt J.A. finds that Russell J. of the Alberta Court of Queen's Bench erred on the question of remedy. Hunt J.A. concludes that the remedy should be limited to the evidence in this case, that is to the sections of the
IRPA
that deal with employment. Also, because she is concerned that, given the complicated wording of these sections, reading in may not be accomplished with adequate precision, Hunt J.A. concludes that it would be preferable to issue a declaration of invalidity and suspend it for a period of time.

In the result, Hunt J.A. would uphold the decision of Russell J. of the Court of Queen's Bench, but would vary the judgment by declaring that
ss. 7(1)
,
8(1)
and
10
of the
IRPA
are of no force and effect to the extent that they fail to extend protection to homosexuals. She would suspend this declaration of invalidity for a period of one year to allow the Alberta Legislature to bring the IRPA into line with the
Charter
.

The appeal is upheld.

McCLUNG J.A.

I.    BACKGROUND

[
1
]    The respondent Delwin Vriend ("Vriend") was employed by King's College in Edmonton. His employment as a laboratory co-ordinator began in December 1987, and in terms of competence and service, was quite satisfactory. However, the College learned that he was homosexual, a fact which he admitted when confronted by the College president. The College is an educational institution which holds strong religious views against homosexuality and homosexual practices. His employment was terminated in January 1991. Vriend protested his employment loss to the Alberta Human Rights Commission ("AHRC") in June 1991. His complaint was rejected on July 10, 1991, on the ground that "sexual orientation" was not a prohibited ground of discrimination under the listed objectives of the
Individual's Rights Protection Act
[R.S.A. 1980, c. I-2] ("
IRPA
") of the Province of Alberta.

[
2
]    In response, Vriend, with the impetus of the respondents Gay and Lesbian Awareness Society of Edmonton ("GALA"), the Gay and Lesbian Community Awareness Centre of Edmonton and Dignity Canada [Dignité] for Gay Catholics and Supporters ("respondents on appeal"), applied by originating notice of motion to the Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta for declaratory relief. The declaration that was sought was effectively an order of the court that the AHRC erred in refusing to investigate and process Vriend's complaint because, it was said, the relevant provisions of the
IRPA
of the Province of Alberta were under-inclusive and infringed
s. 15(1)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
[Part I of the
Constitution Act, 1982,
being Schedule B of the
Canada Act 1982
(U.K.),
1982, c. 11
] ("
Charter
"). The specific infringement alleged was that the omission of "sexual orientation" from the protections of the

Charter

Since the argument in this appeal was heard "sexual orientation" has been recognized by the Supreme Court of Canada as an analogous ground within
s. 15(1)
:
Egan
v.
Canada
,

1995 CanLII 98 (SCC)

[1995] 2 S.C.R. 513
,
124 D.L.R. (4th) 609
.

Section 15(1)
of the
Charter
reads:

15(1) Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.

[
4
]    The Queen's Bench proceedings came on for hearing before Russell J. (as she then was) on February 28, 1994. They concluded by the issuance of her reasons for judgment on April 12, 1994 [reported
1994 CanLII 8949 (AB QB)

20 C.H.R.R. D/358

[
5

1.    That she could judicially notice that homosexuals suffer from discrimination, although no admissible evidence touching the presence or absence of discrimination against homosexuals had been led.

2.    That "sexual orientation" is a ground analogous to those grounds enumerated in the equality declarations found in
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.

3.    Section[s] 2(1), 3, 4, 7(1) and 10 of the
IRPA
infringe
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
because of their failure to include and enumerate "sexual orientation" as a prohibited ground of discrimination.

4.    The absence of "sexual orientation" as a prohibited ground so constitutionally undermined the "under inclusive" declaratory provisions of the
IRPA
and not being defensible under
s. 1
of the
Charter
,
were
ultra vires
the Legislature of the Province of Alberta.

5.    That the appropriate judicial remedy for the constitutional infirmities of the
IRPA
was not to declare them to be of no force and effect, but to include "sexual orientation" by reading it "in," as though it was a legislated head of discrimination, fully akin to race, religious beliefs, colour, gender, physical ability, ancestry or place of origin of a person or class of persons — other categories already found in the
IRPA.

[
6
]    The formal order that issued following the rendering of the judgment was that the disputed provisions of the
IRPA
"... be interpreted, applied and administered as though they contained the words "sexual orientation."

[
7
]    The provisions of the
IRPA
held by Russell J. to be under-inclusive, and therefore constitutionally defective, may be summarized as follows.

1.    Section 2(1) prohibiting discrimination in public notices because of race, religious beliefs, colour, gender, physical disabilities, mental disabilities, age, ancestry, or place of origin.

2.    Sections 3 and 4 prohibiting discrimination in public accommodation and in tenancy, respectively, because of race, religious beliefs, colour, gender, physical disability, mental disability, ancestry or place of origin.

3.    Section[s] 7(1) and 10 prohibiting discrimination in employment and trade unions respectively because of race, religious beliefs, colour, gender, physical disability, mental disability, marital status, age, ancestry or place of origin.

[
8

On November 7, 1994, six organizations applied for, and were granted, intervener status in the appeal. 9
]    After two days of oral submissions the judgment of the Court was reversed.

II.    IS THE IRPA ANSWERABLE, AS IT STANDS, TO THE CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS?

[
10
]    I am left with the conclusion that the Alberta Legislature's exclusion of "sexual orientation" from the enumerated discrimination prohibitions of the
IRPA
does not leave the
IRPA
in so clearly an unconstitutional state that the courts can intervene, through the agency of the
Charter
,
to strike it down, let alone rewrite it.

[
11
]    Simply stated, and notwithstanding
Egan
v.
Canada
, supra,
the omission of the phrase "sexual orientation" by the elected lawmakers of this province as one of the declared discrimination commandments of the
IRPA
,
does not amount to governmental action for the purpose of
s. 32(1)
of the
Charter
.
To clarify the point I wish to make, s. 32(1) of the
Charter
is repeated:

32(1) This
Charter
applies

(a)    to the Parliament and government of Canada in respect of all matters within the authority of Parliament including all matters relating to the Yukon Territory and Northwest Territories; and

(b)    to the legislature and government of each province in respect of
all matters within the authority
of the legislature of each province. [Emphasis added.]

[
12
]    This appeal lies at the uneasy junction of the autonomy of the Legislative Assembly of the Province of Alberta and the implementation of minority, here homosexual, rights. It is a confrontive [
sic
] setting that is backdropped by threats and promises, shrill proclamations, religious and familial forbiddance, the prerogatives of Alberta's Legislature, the limits of their subsequent judicial edit, and what is condemned as the avoidant [
sic
] posture of the Legislative Assembly of the Province of Alberta toward the resolution of a pressing social problem.

[
13
]    The submission that succeeded before Russell J. seems to have drawn its coordinates from the proposition that the enumerated and any emerging analogous grounds contemplated by
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
must be mirrored in any rights legislation passed by the provinces. Implicit in her conclusions is that if the subordinate rights legislation of the provinces and the territories do not perfectly reflect the federal
Charter,
it is constitutionally bad, must be remedied and can be remedied by judge's order. I do not accept those conclusions for the reasons which follow.

[
14
]    Nothing in the
IRPA
,
as passed by the Province of Alberta, purports to draw distinctions between heterosexuals and homosexuals. Nothing in the declarations of the
IRPA
invites or promotes differing social impact, or its expectation, upon homosexuals as opposed to heterosexuals. In fact, the
IRPA
extends full protection to heterosexuals and homosexuals alike who may be discriminated against on the grounds presently specified. No protection is afforded by the legislation to heterosexuals which is simultaneously denied to homosexuals. To me this forces the conclusion that the Legislative Assembly of the Province of Alberta has acted in an even-handed way. The
IRPA
in its silence simply deputes an issue of private conduct to private, not governmental, resolution. This is no more constitutionally unacceptable, for example, than the current decision of the federal, and most provincial governments, to decline any further legislative sorties into the legitimacy of pregnancy termination, relegating the issues surrounding it to private resolution.

[
15
]    In order to establish a
s. 15(1)
constitutional infringement by otherwise valid provincial legislation, it is necessary to demonstrate two things. Firstly, that equal treatment of the class allegedly discriminated against, here the homosexual community, is not furnished before or under the law and, secondly, that the impugned law, here the
IRPA
,
has a discriminatory impact due to — in this case — the analogous
s. 15(1)
ground of "sexual orientation." However, the existing language of the
IRPA
does not draw or invite distinction, let alone discrimination, arising from "sexual orientation," the result of which levies burdens, limitations or disadvantages on the homosexual community. Nor does it deny or limit access to opportunities or benefits that are available to the heterosexual component of the populace. Alberta has not promoted, nor has it prohibited. That is the argument of the appellant Crown and I am persuaded by it.

[
16
]    In its current state, the
IRPA
leaves heterosexuals the choice of contracting with, or employing, homosexuals. It does not force them to do so under pain of the imposition of the sanctions of the
IRPA.
Similarly, homosexuals may employ, contract, or deal with heterosexuals as they choose. Is this exercise of private choice,
ipso facto,
discriminatory? It was not proved in the record. Russell J. found that there was no proof of discriminatory impact in the evidence before her. Hence she was driven to judicially notice its existence as an "indisputable social reality." Resort to "judicial and social comment" and legislation found in other jurisdictions fortified her finding. Her reliance on extra-provincial legislation as an evidentiary foundation aside, it must still be concluded that the impact of the
IRPA,
in its unaltered wording, is the same upon the homosexual segment of Alberta's population as it is upon the heterosexual segment. There is nothing in the record that we have been given that proves that any "indisputable social reality" has or will be exacerbated by the neutral silence of the present
IRPA.

[
17
]    Measured against the backdrop of
Charter

s. 32(1)(b)
— the promise of the provinces and the two territories to dwell within
Charter
perimeters — Alberta has simply not exercised its "authority" (in the way one group of citizens demands), with respect to a "matter" (behaviour that is common to that group). The argument of the appellant emphasized that in the subordinate rights legislation now found in thirteen Canadian jurisdictions (ten provinces, two territories, the federal
Charter of Rights
and the federal
Human Rights Act
[R.S.C. 1985, c. H-6]), there is nothing approaching unanimity in the declared heads of discrimination that these various statutes raise. While there is unanimous condemnation, in all the statutes to which we referred, against discrimination on the grounds of race, colour, sex, age and disability, there is no common or general legislative front against discrimination arising from sexual orientation, national or ethnic origin, religion, pregnancy, marital status, ancestry, political belief, creed, nationality/citizenship, criminal convictions, family status, place of origin, source of income, alcohol/drug dependency, civil status, language, social origin, or condition and place of residence. All of these are declared heads of discrimination in one or more, but not all, of the legislative regimes I have mentioned.

[
18
]    That other jurisdictions do not have to, and do not, emulate the
Charter or Rights and Freedoms
in their legislative responses simply reflects the latitude that must be allowed local lawmakers, especially the provinces, to implement their powers under
s. 92
of the
Constitution Act
[1867 (U.K.), 30 & 31 Vict., c. 3]. The appellant is supported in this by the monition of the internationally-credited human rights jurist L'Heureux-Dubé J. who recognized, when writing
in
McKinney
v.
University of Guelph
,

1990 CanLII 60 (SCC)
,
[1990] 3 S.C.R. 229
at 436
[13 C.H.R.R. D/171 at D/310–D/311, paras. 415–16], that:

I agree with the proposition that human rights legislation has a purpose consistent with that of the
Charter
itself, the promotion of human rights. It has been argued that since such legislation operates in an area which otherwise would remain unaffected by the
Charter
(private transactions), then the least rigid and most flexible standard of review under the
Charter
should be applied. I admit that there is, in fact, a delicate balance to be achieved. The
Charter
should serve to prevent overt discrimination in human rights legislation, but it should not be applied in such a manner as to discourage the use of such legislation by the provinces, or to interfere with a legitimate provincial legislative decision not to provide rights in a given area.

However, there are limits within which this approach should apply. For example, in my view, if the provinces chose to enact human rights legislation which only prohibited discrimination on the basis of sex, and not age, this legislation could not be held to violate the
Charter
.
However, where, as in the present case, the legislation prohibits discrimination on the basis of age, and then defines "age" in a manner that denies this protection to a significant segment of the population, then the
Charter
should apply. Thus, if the province chooses to grant a right, it must grant that right in conformity with the
Charter.

[
19
]    While
in
McKinney
, supra,
L'Heureux-Dubé J. was writing in dissent on the question of whether the
Charter
had any office to serve in the university community, her affirmation of provincial sovereignty in the posting of rights within provincial legislation, by itself, must result in the allowance of the present appeal. L'Heureux-Dubé's analysis is precise in its application and its limits. It is constitutionally workable. It was hardly pronounced
per incuriam.
On the issue at hand it is authority that inescapably binds this Court and the Court of Queen's Bench. With respect, Russell J.'s conclusion sweeps within its condemnation anything falling short of federal initiatives declared under
s. 15(1)
. Such a tenet, even in rights matters, would prove to be a debacle for the autonomy of provincial lawmaking. As well, it contradicts L'Heureux-Dubé J.'s
McKinney
formula.

[
20
]    Clearly, the content of the
IRPA
,
as it presently reads, is neutral, non-aligned and inclines to neither the homosexual nor the heterosexual communities. "Sexual orientation" is not mentioned at all. As L'Heureux-Dubé J. warned, if the provinces, in passing subordinate rights legislation, had purported to grant only token or abridged rights to homosexuals (say by limiting those rights to those who occupy same-sex relationships of no less than two years' duration), then, presumably, standards comporting with those found in the
Charter
would apply and the provisions would be barred. But the province, as it is allowed to do, has here positioned itself in a silent, disengaged and isolationist stance on the matter of the
IRPA
and "sexual orientation." When they choose silence provincial legislatures need not march to the
Charter
drum. In a constitutional sense they need not march at all. That is hardly to say that the governments of the day will not have to answer later to the voters for such a stance. That is as it should be. But in the interim, should Mr. Vriend choose to challenge what he feels is his unlawful dismissal from King's College by litigation rather than by legislation, he will find no obstacle in his path which arises from any law of Alberta favouring either homosexual or heterosexual status. The
IRPA,
as it stands, violates no capitulary of the
Constitution Act,
including the
Charter.
Clearly it is legislation touching property and civil rights, subjects squarely within the competence of the provincially-elected representatives of the people of Alberta.

[
21
]    One of the apprehensions escorting this case is that unless a bar against discrimination because of sexual orientation is specified in the
IRPA
,
homosexuals in Alberta will stand the risk of being summarily dismissed from their existing employment without cause and without remedy. This
in terrorem
argument should not only be addressed but buried. All contracts, including contracts of employment or rental accommodation, can only be lawfully terminated before their completion for violation of their fundamental terms, proven or implied. There may be cases where the heterosexuality of one of the parties is essential to a contract's fulfillment but they would be rare and such a provision, to qualify as a fundamental term, would have to be known to the parties from the outset.

[
22
]    Legislatures, including the Parliament of Canada, need not, and do not enter every morally-eruptive social controversy and attempt to resolve it by statutory remedy. The experience of government has shown that many of the day's major social conflicts may well find their own level of community resolution in time without legislative, let alone needless judicial, prod as the acceptance of wider social mores within Canadian society continues. Canadians of deeper memory will recall W.L. Mackenzie King who, as Prime Minister, turned eschewment of insoluble political conflict into lasting political artistry. So did the astute Sir John A. Macdonald, who did not earn his sobriquet "Old Tomorrow" by any habit of impulsive legislation.

[
23
]    With due deference, Canada's judges would do well to observe similar restraint in their own work,
Charter
or otherwise. When considering the assumption of legislative initiatives (
Rodriguez
v.
B.C. (A.G.),

1993 CanLII 75 (SCC)
,
[1993] 3 S.C.R. 519
at 589 (Sopinka J.)
):

... the Court must be conscious of its proper role in the constitutional make-up of our form of democratic government and not seek to make fundamental changes to long-standing policy on the basis of general constitutional principles and its own view of the wisdom of legislation. On the other hand, the Court has not only the power but the duty to deal with this question if it appears that the
Charter
has been violated”¦ The principles of fundamental justice leave a great deal of scope for personal judgment and the Court must be careful that they do not become principles which are of fundamental justice in the eye of the beholder only.

While he was addressing the limits of "fundamental justice" as employed in
s. 7
of the
Charter
,
Sopinka J.'s curial alert, which I have quoted, should not be artificially distinguished. It applies with equal, if not more, force when legisceptical Canadian judges decide to strike down constitutionally assembled laws in favour of their own, substituting their own vision of the ideal statute in place of that which has been democratically endorsed by the electors.

[
24
]    Under the
IRPA,
as it stands, there is no burden imposed upon homosexuals or any other minority that is not mentioned in its declaration. The
IRPA
neither subjugates, nor promotes, the homosexual community. The Alberta Legislature through the
IRPA
has simply remained silent. But it has also remained silent in other especially contentious and morally-laden issues such as physician-assisted suicide, reproductive rights for women (as opposed to their cost), genetic engineering and, to date, the right to work, to give a few examples. Adopting the maxim "all silent, all condemned" as a constitutional tool available to judges to reject a perfectly valid statute because they believe it does not go far enough in their view of the ideal society, breaks new, and in my view, undesirable ground. Is it constitutionally inexcusable for the Alberta government to decline to choose between the platforms of the divinely-driven right and the rights-euphoric, cost-scoffing left, by refusing to order people of either sexual base to listen to government as to when they must forget that sexuality and contract together? If provincial legislation does not go far enough, instead of too far, for the
Charter of Rights
,
surely the provincial legislature should not be ordered to specifically perform some later federal mandate on the subject. Must it pass and proclaim as a consequence of not legislating to begin with? Surely not. Such a new judicial
mandamus,
lordly directed to autonomous, co-equal branches of government (legislatures), as if they were some inferior tribunal, releases fresh and limitless concepts which undermine the compartmental theorems that support present Canadian constitutional practice.

[
25
]    The order paper of the Alberta Legislature is not to be dictated, even incidentally, by federally appointed judges brandishing the
Charter
.
While any legislative product touching governmental activity is, of course, now subject to
Charter
scrutiny under its
ss. 32
and
52
, the practice of judicially upgrading that product should be strictly disciplined. This is because of the spectre of constitutionally-hyperactive judges in the future pronouncing all of our emerging rights laws and according to their own values; judicial appetites, too, grow with the eating. Equally undesirable is the prospect of Canada's legislators, painfully aware of later electoral rejection for backing the wrong political horses, further acquiescing in the growing (and painless) expedient of shipping awkward political questions to the judiciary for decision, thus reserving to themselves the privilege of possible later disclaimer.

[
26
]    That "sexual orientation" is so obviously a divisive issue, like right-to-life or euthanasia (issues which are also touched by the declarations of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
), does not, by its gravity alone, force the hand of the legislator. You cannot legislate morality or successfully order people to love each other. Both are battered old bromides. But as practical considerations, both survive. As Thomas Reed, long-time speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives warned a century ago, "... One of the greatest delusions in the world is the hope that the evils in this world are to be cured by legislation."

[
27
]    As I have said, Alberta's legislative calendar must be set by the elected representatives of voting Albertans, not outside agencies. Clearly the
Charter
,
the supreme law of Canada, must monitor Alberta's legislative products but only after they are proclaimed to be in force. Legislative inactivity is hardly law; statutes become law only when they are proclaimed, not before. It is at that time alone that the remedies
discussed in
Schachter
v.
Canada

(1992),
1992 CanLII 74 (SCC)
,
93 D.L.R. (4th) 1
at 34 (S.C.C.)
can be used to refine even "under-inclusive" human rights legislation. But legislative silence remains an imperative of choice for the provincial legislatures, clearly so when their considered choice is to table questions of private activity to private resolution, as Alberta has done here. The ideals of the process of legislation include discoverability, clarity, balanced application and the accountability of both legislators and their legislation. Judges castigating legislatures for what they
fail
to produce is an impatience that is difficult to reconcile with those ideals.

[
28
]    Constitutional experts, even in the heady human rights elation of the early 1980s, never anticipated a scheme of government wherein federal judges wielding the
Charter
could dictate provincial legislation while pretextually offering mere constitutional scrutiny. Recently, Major J. reminded the nation's superior courts of the importance of maintaining their traditional restraint
in
Zeitel
v.
Ellscheid
,

1994 CanLII 82 (SCC)
,
[1994] 2 S.C.R. 142
. Citing E.A. Dreidger,
Construction of Statutes,
2d ed. (Toronto: Butterworths, 1983) at 86, Major J. warned that:

Recognition of the proper roles of the legislature and the judiciary requires that the courts give effect to the plain meaning of the words of a duly enacted scheme. It is beyond the power of a court to interfere in a carefully crafted legislative scheme merely because it does not approve of the result produced by a statute in a particular case.

[
29
]    Other declarations of the need for judicial self-restraint are easily assembled. Major J. was echoing Chambre J., two hundred years earlier, in
Grigby
v.
Oakes

(1801),
2 Bos. & Pul. 526
,
126 E.R. 1420
, in which case the Court discussed the pursuit of the perfect statute and cautioned, "... If the legislature has not gone far enough, it is for them, not for us, to remedy the defect." This proposition is fully tied to the general jurisprudence of Alberta, "The responsibility to see that the statute law is just is on the Legislature, not on the Courts,"
Richert Co.
v.
Forbes
,

1937 CanLII 235 (AB SCAD)
,
[1937] 3 W.W.R. 632
at 635 (Alta. C.A., Harvey C.J.A.)
. Yet we judges insist on mechanically invading the legislative arena because human rights may be involved. Seemingly the nobility of the occasion now expiates the old judicial sin of repealing, even amending, legislation under the cloak of merely interpreting it.

[
30
]    The
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
was adopted by the provinces, in part, to restrain the activity of government where that governmental activity encroached upon the freedoms that were declared and protected by it. The
Charter
,
when
s. 32(1)
(b) is reviewed, applies when government, here Alberta, exceeds its "authority" with respect to a "matter." In proclaiming the
IRPA
the Alberta Legislature has done nothing to "authorize," promote, or even condone, discrimination resulting from the "matter" of "sexual orientation." In that "matter," here the legislature has chosen to remain silent. It has chosen silence on this issue as it has chosen silence in response to some of the other live social issues of the day. But silence is a compartment of the Alberta Legislature's own Charter. The
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
was not adopted by the provinces to promote the federal extraction of subsidiary legislation from them but only to police it once it is proclaimed — if it is proclaimed. Before it can contravene
ss. 32(1)(b)
and
52
of the
Charter,
the Legislative Assembly of the Province of Alberta must act. Only then is it answerable to the corrective hand of s. 96 judges.

[
31
]    Because I apprehend no constitutional violation flowing from the legislature's disengagement from the issue of "sexual orientation," it is not necessary to extensively address
s. 1
of the
Charter
,
beyond associating myself, respectfully, with Sopinka J.'s conclusion
in
Egan
v.
Canada
, supra,
the same-sex benefits case, where he wrote:

... as La Forest J. did
in
McKinney
,
that I am "not prepared to say that the course adopted by the Legislature, in the social and historical context through which we are now passing, is not one that reasonably balances competing social demands which our society must address."

[
32
]    I have reached this conclusion mindful of the objectives of the two schools of legitimate social concern that have forced this case. Alberta's legislative response was not disproportionate. I am unable to conclude that it was a forbidden, let alone a reversible, legislative response for the Province of Alberta to step back from the validation of homosexual relations, including sodomy, as a protected and fundamental right, thereby "... rebutting a millennia of moral teaching":
Bowers
v.
Hardwick,
92 L. Ed. 2d. 140 (U.S.S.C. 1986), per Burger C.J. at 150. It is far from edifying but still conformable with fact, that, as homosexual-rights advocate Andrew Sullivan has conceded (
Virtually Normal,
Sullivan, Alfred Knopf, 1995):

”¦ For many people in Western societies, and most others, the sexual and emotional entanglement of two people of the same gender is a moral enormity. They find such behaviour abhorrent, even threatening; and while, in a liberal society, they may be content to leave such people alone, they draw the line at being told they cannot avoid their company in the workplace or in renting housing to them.

[
33
]    If the Provincial Legislature, even in its disengagement from the issue of "sexual orientation," under s. 32(1) is still answerable to the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
,
as my colleague Hunt J.A. has concluded, it must still be borne in mind that
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
was not meant to be a guarantee of equality in the "general or abstract" sense:
Andrews
v.
Law Society of British Columbia
,

1989 CanLII 2 (SCC)
,
[1989] 1 S.C.R. 143
[10 C.H.R.R. D/5719]. Legislation (or its silence), even facially neutral legislation, must be examined for its real impact upon the minority said to be adversely affected. Here I take as authoritative the analytical guidance offered by Iacobucci J.
in
Symes
v.
Canada
,

1993 CanLII 55 (SCC)
,
[1993] 4 S.C.R. 695
at 764
:

If the adverse effects analysis is to be coherent, it must not assume that a statutory provision [or the absence of one] has an effect which is not proved. We must take care to distinguish between effects which are wholly caused, or which are contributed to, by an impugned provision [or its absence] and those social circumstances which exist independently of such a provision. [Parenthetical additions are mine.]

[
34
]    I cannot conclude that the considered but muted legislative response of the Legislative Assembly of the Province of Alberta to the inclusion of "sexual orientation" into the
IRPA
does anything but respect this principle. The effect of the Alberta legislative stance is that in the areas touched by the
IRPA,
homosexuals and heterosexuals may contract or decline to contract with each other without legislated incentives. If, as Russell J. has found, the homosexual community suffers inequality for the reasons she has given, such inequality exists independently of the
IRPA,
or any other Alberta statute, and cannot be a legislative fallout:
Eldridge
v.
British Columbia

(1995),
1995 CanLII 2964 (BC CA)
,
125 D.L.R. (4th) 323 (B.C.C.A.)
.

[
35
]    I am at least diffident to any judicial approach which finds a
Charter
-barred distinction by identifying (or assuming) adverse effects on an individual or a group from an apparently neutral statute which neither confers nor denies benefits to, or withdraws protection from, any Canadian. That is a constitutional adventure that has no rational limits and one which would place impossible shackles upon provincial or territorial legislatures, not only in human rights legislation but in all legislation which impacts unequally — which most legislation does.

III.   REMEDY

[
36
]    If I am wrong, and the
IRPA
,
as it stands, is constitutionally undermined by
s. 15(1)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
,
I am of the view that Russell J. still erred in her resort to judicial "reading up" as the relief that was forced in the matter. There was another, preferable, response. The
Act
should have been declared unconstitutional and invalid because it did not mirror
Charter
s. 15(1), without more. That was the end of the appropriate judicial function in this case, subject only to the following. The declaration of invalidity should have been stayed to provide a grace period to permit legislative, not judicial, repair. I express no view on Russell J. taking judicial notice, in the absence of evidence, of discrimination and on her finding that members of the homosexual community, whether strident or stolid, have, for the purpose of the
Charter
s. 15(1), traditionally been and currently are discriminated against. That issue, one extensively argued before us, has been overtaken, at least in law, by the intervening judgments of
the Supreme Court of Canada in
Egan
v.
Canada
, supra.
Beyond that, I say nothing as well of the respondent's answer to the appellant's concerns that the term "sexual orientation" is limited to "traditional" homosexual practices shared by consenting adults, and its
IRPA
inclusion would never be raised as a permissive shield sheltering other practices, both heterosexual and homosexual, commonly regarded as deviance in both communities. It is pointless to deny that the Dahmer, Bernardo and Clifford Robert Olsen prosecutions have recently heightened public concern about violently aberrant sexual configurations and how they find expression against their victims.

[
37
]    If the
IRPA,

... I have no doubt that women disproportionally incur the

[

or to interfere with a legitimate provincial legislative decision not to provide rights in a given area

However, there are limits within which this approach should apply. For example, in my view, if the province[s] chose to enact human rights legislation which only prohibited discrimination on the basis of sex, and not age,

[
76
]    The present case is one in which the statute is silent on the matter of sexual orientation. It therefore does not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation.

[
77
]    It is not enough to say, first, that homosexuals do suffer and have historically suffered from discrimination, and, second, that the
IRPA
provides protection against discrimination on certain grounds, but not on the basis of sexual orientation. The respondent's argument posits a distinction between grounds that are included in the
IRPA
and grounds which are not. That argument does
not

distinguishes between,

(1)   individuals who suffer discrimination and
can

(2)   individuals who are discriminated against on the basis of their sexual orientation, who cannot access the
IRPA

It cannot be asserted that this is a law which discriminates on the
basis
of sexual orientation; at most all that the
IRPA

[
78
]    I do not accept that
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
may be read so broadly that if legislatures enter into the field of human rights legislation at all, they must extend protection and benefits to no less an extent that is expressed (and even unexpressed but implied) under s. 15(1) of the
Charter.
Nor do I believe that s. 15(1) of the
Charter
requires human rights legislation to place all disadvantaged individuals and groups on an identical footing. If special legislative protection is provided to individuals against discrimination on the basis of, say, race, s. 15(1) of the
Charter
does not automatically require that such protection be extended against discrimination on the basis of, for example, age, sex or religion, even though it can be demonstrated that discrimination on those grounds exists. All statutes conferring benefits, tangible or otherwise, or affording protection, are bound to impact differently on different individuals and groups, even if the statute is expressed in neutral language. The
s. 15(1)
inquiry must be directed at whether a law distinguishes in a discriminatory manner on the basis of a prohibited or analogous ground, not whether the law fails to provide protection against every enumerated and analogous ground of discrimination.

[
79
]    My conclusions are also supported by the reasons of Hollinrake J.A.

125 D.L.R. (4th) 323 (B.C.C.A.)

In establishing the impact of the legislation there must be a distinction drawn between those effects which can be attributed to the legislation and those which exist independently of it.

Hearing people in the absence of the legislation would be in the similar position of having the responsibility of making payment to their doctors. The legislation removes the responsibility of both the hearing and the deaf to make payment to their doctors. This is the impact of the legislation on both the deaf and the hearing. provides protection against some categories of discrimination, just as it is true that the statute at issue

by reason of such a distinction
. [Emphasis added.]

I do not agree that this suffices to make out a violation of

of the
Charter
.
Neither expressly nor in effect does the

Charter
on this basis.

[
84
]    It has often been said that the
Charter
is a remedial document and should be interpreted generously. However, it was and remains directed at regulating legislation and government action, not private activity. The effects of the respondent's argument would be to force all federal and provincial human rights legislation, as well as countless other pieces of benefit or protection conferring legislation, to not only
not offend

s. 15(1)
, but to
mirror
it. That is, all legislation would have to provide benefits and protections equally to everyone (except legislation which could be "saved" under s. 1 or s. 15(2)). In turn the effect would be that
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
would directly govern private activity, by defining all that must be included in human rights and other legislation. The cautionary words of McIntyre J. at 288–89 [D/5739, para. 41745] of
Andrews, supra,
bear repeating:

[s. 15(1)] is not a general guarantee of equality; it does not provide for equality between individuals or groups within society in a general or abstract sense, nor does it impose on individuals or groups an obligation to accord equal treatment to others.

So too, the following admonition of La Forest J.
in
McKinney
, supra
(at 676 [D/223, para. 130], should be heeded:

”¦ generally, the courts should not lightly use the
Charter
to second-guess legislative judgment as to just how quickly it should proceed in moving forward towards the ideal of equality. The courts should adopt a stance that encourages legislative advances in the protection of human rights. Some of the steps adopted may well fall short of perfection, but as earlier mentioned, the recognition of human rights emerges slowly out of the human condition, and short or incremental steps may at times be a harbinger of a developing right, a further step in the long journey towards full and ungrudging recognition of the dignity of the human person.

[
85
]    In sum, I find that the learned trial judge erred in holding that the impugned provisions of the
IRPA
violate
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.
Where it is legislation that is being attacked, there can be no violation of
s. 15(1)
unless that legislation creates a distinction, directly or by adverse effect, between individuals on the basis of an enumerated or analogous ground. Here, the
IRPA
cannot be said to create a distinction between individuals on the basis of sexual orientation, either directly or in effect. It prohibits some grounds of discrimination, and does not prohibit others. To the extent that this is a "distinction," it is simply a distinction between grounds which are included and grounds which are not. In no way does the
IRPA
distinguish between individuals of different sexual orientations. While the social reality may be that those of a homosexual orientation are often discriminated against, s. 15(1) of the
Charter
is limited in its application to legislation and government action. The legislation at issue here, the
IRPA,
simply does not infringe the
s. 15(1)
guarantee to the "equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination" on the basis of sexual orientation.

[
86
]    As a result, I would allow the appeal and set aside the declaration made by the learned trial judge.

[
87

IRPA
does not violate
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
,
it is not necessary for me to determine whether or not the learned trial judge was correct to "read" sexual orientation into the
Act.
Had I found otherwise, however, I would agree with the reasoning of Hunt J.A. that this is not an appropriate case for "reading in." This is a matter where the Legislature must decide, within the terms of
s. 15(1)
, the contours of any protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. As such, if
s. 15(1)
were infringed by the failure to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, the most appropriate remedy would be to declare
ss. 7(1)
, [8](1) and 10 of the
IRPA
invalid. The operation of such declaration should then be suspended for a period of one year, to permit the Legislature to amend the legislation.

SECTION 15(1) OF THE CHARTER

I.    Generally

[
97

Andrews
v.

1989 CanLII 2 (SCC)

[1989] 2 W.W.R. 289

[
98

The court must first determine whether the claimant has shown that one of the four basic equality rights has been denied (i.e., equality before the law, equality under the law, equal protection of the law and equal benefit of the law). This inquiry will focus largely on whether the law has drawn a distinction (intentionally or otherwise) between the claimant and others, based on personal characteristics. Next, the court must determine whether the denial can be said to result in "discrimination". This second inquiry will focus largely on whether the differential treatment has the effect of imposing a burden, obligation or disadvantage not imposed upon others or of withholding or limiting access to opportunities, benefits and advantages available to others. Furthermore, in determining whether the claimant's
s. 15(1)
rights have been infringed, the court must consider whether the personal characteristic in question falls within the grounds enumerated in the section or within an analogous ground, so as to ensure that the claim fits within the overall purpose of s. 15 — namely, to remedy or prevent discrimination against groups subject to stereotyping, historical disadvantage and political and social prejudice in Canadian society.

[
99

[
100

of some cases

[
