R.S.C. 1985, c. O-9, which limited certain benefits to persons of the opposite sex who lived together. Egan and Nesbit, homosexuals who had cohabited since 1948, claimed that this definition discriminated on the basis of sexual orientation. Drawing upon the analysis of Gonthier J. in
Miron, supra,
La Forest J., for Lamer C.J. and Major and Gonthier JJ., concluded that there had been no breach of
s. 15(1)
. Cory J., on behalf of Iacobucci J., concluded that there had been a
s. 15(1)
breach, with Sopinka J. concurring in his analysis. Their approach to
s. 15(1)
is similar to the approach taken in
Miron
by McLachlin J.;
in
Egan
,
she expressed substantial agreement with Cory and Iacobucci JJ., based upon her reasons in
Miron.
L'Heureux-Dubé J. stated that, while she agreed with much of what was said by Cory and Iacobucci JJ., as well as with their result, she preferred a different approach.

[
103
]    Although the split on the Court in the third case was slightly different from the first two, the same conceptual approaches are evident.
Thibaudeau, supra,
involved the validity of a provision in the
Income Tax Act
that required custodial parents to include as income any amounts received for the support of those children. Gonthier J. applied his
Miron, supra,
approach to conclude that there was no breach; Sopinka and La Forest JJ. agreed. Cory and Iacobucci JJ. agreed with the result, based not on Gonthier J.'s analysis but rather based on their
approach in
Miron
and
Egan
, supra.
Although they agreed with the approach of McLachlin J. in this case, they disagreed with her result. In dissent, both McLachlin J. and L'Heureux-Dubé J. found that
s. 15(1)
had been breached, each following the analysis they had used in the other cases.

[
104
]    From this, it may be concluded that Cory, Iacobucci, and McLachlin JJ. have taken one approach to
s. 15(1)
, an approach that seems to have been accepted by Sopinka J.
in
Egan
, supra,
and that he clearly accepted in
Miron, supra.

In
Thibaudeau
, supra,
Sopinka J. agreed with Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ., without stating any preference as to the form of analysis. Lamer C.J., Gonthier, Major and La Forest JJ. have followed a second type of analysis, while L'Heureux-Dubé J. has taken a third. Thus, it is not clear that a majority view as to "discrimination" for the purposes of
s. 15(1)
exists on the Supreme Court of Canada. As I understand them, the three approaches are these.

A.    Approach No. 1: The McLachlin, Cory, Iacobucci JJ. (and Probably Sopinka J.) View

[
105
]    Following on
Andrews, supra,
the
s. 15(1)
analysis requires two steps.

1.    Has there been a denial of one of the four equality rights, due to a distinction created by the questioned law? Has the challenged law drawn a distinction between the claimant and others, based on personal characteristics?

2.    Does that distinction constitute discrimination? To show discrimination, it must be shown that the denial of equality rests upon one of the enumerated grounds in
s. 15(1)
or an analogous ground, and that "the unequal treatment is based on the stereotypical application of presumed group of personal characteristics" (
Miron, supra,
at para. 128).

[
106
]    As regards the second step, there may be situations where distinctions made on enumerated or analogous grounds are non-discriminatory, for example, where the distinction does not engage the purpose of
s. 15(1)
, which purpose as stated in
Miron, supra,
at para. 131 is "to prevent the violation of human dignity and freedom by imposing limitations, disadvantages or burdens through the stereotypical application of presumed group characteristics rather than on the basis of individual merit, capacity, or circumstance." Similarly, there may be cases where there is a distinction on an enumerated or analogous ground, but where it does not have the effect of imposing a real disadvantage in the social and political context of the claim. Cases where a distinction made on an enumerated or analogous ground does not amount to discrimination will, however, be rare.

[
107
]    The proponents of this view take issue with the Gonthier/La Forest JJ. position that discrimination under
s.15(1)
may be rebutted by a finding that the ground on which the equal treatment is denied is relevant to the legislative goals or functional values underlying the impugned law. The McLachlin
et al.
group consider that "relevance" is only one part of the discrimination test. According to their view, if the basis of the distinction is clearly irrelevant to the functional values of the legislation, then the distinction will be discriminatory. If the basis of the distinction is relevant to the legislative aims, then it is necessary to go on and examine "the effect or impact of the distinction in the social and economic context of the legislation and the lives of the individuals it touches," per McLachlin J. in
Miron, supra,
at para. 133. She says that by defining the functional values underlying the legislation in terms of the alleged discriminatory ground, the basis of the legislative distinction will necessarily be relevant to the legislative aim. In her opinion, this is a form of circular reasoning which can be broken out of only by examining the impact of the distinction in terms of the members of the targeted group. The social and economic context must be studied to see whether the impugned distinction perpetuates undesirable stereotyping which s. 15(1) aims to eradicate.

B.    Approach No. 2: The Gonthier, La Forest, Major JJ. and Lamer C.J. View

[
108
]    According to this view, there are three steps in a
s. 15(1)
analysis.

1.    Has the law drawn a distinction between the claimant and others?

2.    Does the distinction result in disadvantage; does the impugned law impose a burden, obligation or disadvantage on a group to which the claimant belongs which it does not impose on others, or does it deny them a benefit that others are granted? At this point the direct or indirect impact of the law must be examined.

3.    Is the distinction based upon an irrelevant personal characteristic that is enumerated in
s. 15(1)
or is analogous thereto? This step comprises two parts:

(a)   What is the personal characteristic shared by the group?

(b)   Is this characteristic relevant to the functional values underlying the legislation?

[
109
]    According to Gonthier J. in
Miron, supra,
at para. 15, "the functional values underlying the law may themselves be discriminatory. Such will be the case where the underlying values are irrelevant to any legitimate legislative purpose."

C.    Approach No. 3: The L'Heureux-Dubé J. View

[
110
]    Madam Justice L'Heureux-Dubé's approach is set out comprehensively
in
Egan
, supra,
where she states at para. 35 that independent content should be given to the term "discrimination" in order to develop
s. 15(1)
. The purpose of the equality right in
s. 15(1)
is to recognize "each person's equal worth as a human being, regardless of individual differences" (para. 36). At para. 39, she states:

To summarize, at the heart of s. 15 is the promotion of a society in which all are secure in the knowledge that they are recognized at law as equal human beings, equally capable, and equally deserving. A person or group of persons has been discriminated [against] within the meaning of
s. 15
of the
Charter
when members of the group have been made to feel, by virtue of the impugned legislative distinction, that they are less capable or less worthy of recognition as human beings or as members of Canadian society, equally deserving of concern, respect, and consideration. These are the core elements of a definition of "discrimination" — a definition that focuses on impact (i.e. discriminatory effect) rather than non-constituent elements (i.e. the grounds of the distinction).

[
111
]    In her view, the "relevance" approach to
s. 15(1)
is untenable. She states at para. 43
in
Egan
, supra,
that this test fails to "take into account the possibility that a distinction that is relevant to the purpose of the legislation may nonetheless still have a discriminatory effect." Moreover, the legislative purpose itself may be discriminatory. Additionally, this approach would place too heavy a burden on the claimant, as the purpose of the legislation is much more likely to be in the knowledge of the government. In her view, relevance is more properly considered under s. 1.

[
112
]    Under her approach, a claimant must show (para. 55) that there is a legislative distinction; that it results in a denial of one of the four equality rights; and that this distinction is discriminatory. At para. 56, she observes that a distinction is discriminatory:

where it is capable of either promoting or perpetuating the view that the individual adversely affected by this distinction is less capable, or less worthy of recognition or value as a human being or as a member of Canadian society, equally deserving of concern, respect and consideration. This examination should be undertaken from a subjective-objective perspective: i.e. from the point of view of the reasonable person, dispassionate and fully apprised of the circumstances, possessed of similar attributes to, and under similar circumstances as, the group of which the rights claimant is a member.

D.    Summary on the Trilogy

[
113
]    At the least, what is clear is that, according to all three approaches, to get under
s. 15(1)
there must be a distinction that gives rise to the interference with one of the four equality rights. Moreover, the distinction must be discriminatory. It is in the approach to "discrimination" that members of the Court appear to differ. One view (explained by La Forest and Gonthier JJ.) is that, if the distinction is relevant to the legislative goals, there will be no discrimination, unless those goals themselves can be said to offend
Charter
values. According to the approach articulated by McLachlin, Cory and Iacobucci JJ., a distinction that is relevant to the legislative goals may still be discriminatory, if it impacts upon the claimant in a way that is contrary to the purpose of
s. 15(1)
, namely, if the distinction stereotypes rather than evaluates based upon individual merit.

II.    The Trial Decision

[
114
]    Russell J. took the position that the protection in the
IRPA
from discrimination on the basis of "gender" (which she said had the same effect as if the word "sex" had been used instead of "gender") was "directly associated" with questions of discrimination based upon sexual orientation. At p. 13 [D/365, para. 49] she said "While there is no obligation on the Province to legislate to prohibit sexual discrimination, when it does so it must provide even-handed protection in a non-discriminatory manner, or justify the exclusion." At least by inference, she analyzed the present case as being similar to
Re Blainey and Ontario Hockey Association

(1986),
1986 CanLII 145 (ON CA)
,
54 O.R. (2d) 513
[
1986 CanLII 6547 (ON CA)
,
7 C.H.R.R. D/3529
] (C.A.); leave to appeal refused [1986] S.C.R. xii and
McKinney, supra.

[
115
]    In
Blainey, supra,
the Ontario Court of Appeal declared invalid s. 19(2) of the Ontario
Human Rights Code, 1981,
S.O. 1981, c. 53. This section stated that a general protection provided by s. 1 of the
Code
(the right to equal services without discrimination because of,
inter alia,
sex) was not infringed "where membership in an athletic organization or participation in an athletic activity is restricted to persons of the same sex." The complainant Blainey had been denied access to the machinery of the Human Rights Commission when the Ontario Hockey Association refused to allow her to play on a boys' hockey team. Dubin J.A. (Morden J.A. concurring) held at p. 526 [D/3539] that s. 19(2) denied Blainey the protection and benefit of complaint and enforcement procedures found in the
Human Rights Code.
As such, it permitted direct discrimination against her, and was inconsistent with
s. 15(1)
. It also resulted in adverse effect discrimination against females because males were not denied the right to full membership and participation in athletic organizations.

[
116
]
In
McKinney
, supra,
a successful attack was made upon
s. 9
(a) of the
Ontario
Human Rights Code.
Section 4(1) of the
Code
provided that everyone has a right to equal treatment with respect to employment "without discrimination because of ... age ..."
Section 9
(a) defined age as 18 or more, except in relation to s. 4(1) where it was defined to mean 18 years or more and less than 65 years. For the majority, La Forest J. held at p. 655 [D/203, para. 76] that this provision of the
Code
violated
s. 15(1)
because it deprived the appellants

of a benefit under the
Code
on the basis of their age, a ground specifically enumerated in the
Charter
.
It must be underlined that
s. 15(1)
expressly guarantees the right to equality [before and under] the law; it also guarantees the right to equal protection of the law.

Reliance was placed upon
Blainey, supra.

[
117
]    In my view,
Blainey
and
McKinney, supra,
involved equality questions of a different context than here. Specifically, they involved cases where general protection from discrimination as to age and sex was extended by the Ontario
Code,
with the protection then limited in ways the courts found to be in breach of
s. 15(1)
.

[
118
]    In this case, I am not convinced that affording protection under the
IRPA
based upon "gender" can be directly associated with providing protection based upon sexual orientation. It was argued by the appellants that gender is a biological matter while sexual orientation has to do with, among other things, behaviour. I am not certain that the issue is so clear-cut.
In
Egan
, supra,
La Forest J. observed at 528 that he had no difficulty accepting the contention that "whether or not sexual orientation is based on biological or physiological factors, which may be a matter of some controversy, it is a deeply personal characteristic that is either unchangeable or changeable only at unacceptable personal costs”¦" Given that there continues to be considerable disagreement about the reasons for sexual orientation, I cannot conclude, as did Russell J., that sexual orientation is akin to gender. Thus, in my view, this case is not like
Blainey
and
McKinney, supra.

III.    Application of Section 15(1) to this Case

A.    Does the IRPA Draw a Distinction between Individuals Based upon their Sexual Orientation?

[
119
]    This case presents an issue that has not yet been decided by the Supreme Court of Canada. The special case is this. The Alberta Legislature has passed a law, the
IRPA,
that offers protection from discrimination to certain groups that have been the victims of discrimination. It does not offer the same protection to another group (homosexuals) that — as the evidence here establishes — have also been the victims of discrimination.

[
120
]    Does the failure of the Legislature to include homosexuals as a protected group amount to the drawing of a distinction between that group and
other
victims of discrimination who have been afforded the protection of the
IRPA?
To put the matter another way, can legislative silence or omission amount to the drawing of a distinction? Essentially, this is the same issue that faced
the Ontario Court of Appeal in
Haig
v.
Canada

(1992),
1992 CanLII 2787 (ON CA)
,
94 D.L.R. (4th) 1
[16 C.H.R.R. D/226], discussed below.

[
121
]    There are at least four possible answers to this question. One is that
s. 15(1)
does not require a government to offer aid to all victims of discrimination. A second is that, having decided to offer protection to some victims of discrimination, a government must offer protection to other victims as well. One ramification of the second approach might be that, having entered the field of human rights, legislatures would have to extend protection on all the
s. 15(1)
enumerated grounds as well as on all analogous grounds. This could be considered an extension of
the approach taken in
Blainey
and
McKinney
, supra.

[
122
]    A third approach is that legislatures cannot avoid a s. 15(1) analysis
merely
because they have failed to extend a protection or benefit to a particular group. In other words, a failure to legislate (or legislative silence or omission) can
of itself
attract
Charter
scrutiny. Whether that failure to act will indeed run afoul of the
Charter
will depend on a number of factors. The most important factors are the
context
of the impugned legislation and whether the
purpose
of the Legislature in failing to act is to encourage or support the distinction that results between groups that are protected and those that are not. As I will discuss presently, there is
dicta
of Wilson J. to support this approach.

[
123
]    A fourth approach might be that the Legislature's failure to act will amount to the drawing of a distinction if the
effect
of the silence is discrimination against certain groups. As discussed below, this seems to be the approach of Krever J.A.
in
Haig
, supra,
and adopted in dissent by Lambert J.A. in
Eldridge
v.
British Columbia,

1995 CanLII 2964 (BC CA)
,
[1995] B.C.J. No. 1168
[reported 125 D.L.R. (4th) 323] (B.C.C.A.). This view may be seen to be based on some of the language of Iacobucci J.
in
Symes
v.
Canada
,

1993 CanLII 55 (SCC)
,
[1993] 4 S.C.R. 695
,
110 D.L.R. (4th) 470
.

[
124
]    For reasons that follow, I prefer the third approach. I conclude in this case that, given the context of the
IRPA
and the facts found by the trial judge, the purpose of the Legislature's failure to protect homosexuals under the
IRPA
is to encourage or support the distinction that exists between homosexuals and other victims of discrimination that are protected by the
IRPA.

[
125
]    Although, as I have said, the Supreme Court of Canada has not specifically addressed the issue here, there is
dicta
that supports the "purpose and context" approach. There are also appellate decisions, as well as other Supreme Court
dicta,
that suggest an "effects" approach. These authorities are as follows.

[
126
]
In
McKinney
, supra,
Wilson J. discussed at 625 [D/293, para. 358] whether s. 9(a) of the
Human Rights Code
infringed the
Charter
.
She said:

It has been argued by the respondents as well as by some of the interveners that this limit upon the reach of the
Code
does not offend the
Charter
because the province was under no obligation to provide any protection against discrimination in the first place. They say that absent such an obligation there is no room for constitutional scrutiny of the state's failure to go far enough in legislating human rights protection.
It is not self-evident to me that government could not be found to be in breach of the
Charter
for failing to act
. Whether the
Constitution
is implicated when the state fails to do something is a question which has plagued the American courts for many years. Indeed, Laurence Tribe has commented that it is precisely when the state has not acted that the court is called upon to make the most difficult determinations regarding the scope of the
Constitution:
see
Constitutional Choices
(Cambridge, 1985) at p. 246
et seq.
Since this is not an instance where the province has completely failed to act, we are happily relieved from deciding such a difficult question on these appeals, and I refrain from doing so. [Emphasis added.]

[
127
]    Wilson J. discussed a similar issue
in
Lavigne
v.
Ontario Public Service Employees Union

(1991),
1991 CanLII 68 (SCC)
,
81 D.L.R. (4th) 545 (S.C.C.)
.
Lavigne
involved the question of whether,
inter alia,
the
Charter
's guarantees of freedom of expression and freedom of association were infringed by compulsory payment of union dues. At p. 569
et seq.
Wilson J. considered whether there was, in that case, sufficient "government action" to bring the case within
s. 32
of the
Charter.
She pointed out that what was at issue was "permissive" legislation, i.e., legislation that allowed the compulsory contribution of dues. She said at pp. 570–71:

On the other hand, it must be recognized that if this court were to hold without qualification that the
Charter
does not apply to permissive legislation, the door would surely be open to widespread abuse at the hands of the government. This court has already acknowledged that
technical avoidance of the application of the
Charter
is to be discouraged
.

By analogy, it is easy to envision that government may avoid its duty to respect the guarantees embodied in the
Charter
through the vehicle of permissive legislation. This, of course, is a result which this court should seek to avoid. What qualifications therefore need to be added to the general principle that permissive statutory provisions standing alone are insufficient to call the
Charter
into play?

As a general observation, I would think that in each case
all the circumstances would have to be carefully examined to determine whether government had significantly encouraged or supported the act which is called into question
. Depending upon the context, the enactment of the permissive provision may indeed support a finding of governmental approval or encouragement of a particular activity sufficient to invoke the protective guarantees of the
Charter
.
[Emphasis added.]

(As this passage reveals, the specific question raised here could also be considered to arise in the context of s. 32. But for reasons already given, I have concluded that the requirements of s. 32 have been met in this case and prefer to treat the issue as a
s. 15(1)
question.)

[
128
]    A contrary view seems to have been taken by L'Heureux-Dubé J.
in
McKinney
, supra,
who, in the course of her s. 1 analysis, observed at 691 [D/310, paras. 415–16]:

I agree with the proposition that human rights legislation has a purpose consistent with that of the
Charter
itself, the promotion of human rights. It has been argued that since such legislation operates in an area which otherwise would remain unaffected by the
Charter
(private transactions), then the least rigid and most flexible standard of review under the
Charter
should be applied. I admit that there is, in fact, a delicate balance to be achieved. The
Charter
should serve to prevent overt discrimination in human rights legislation, but it should not be applied in such a manner as to discourage the use of such legislation by the provinces, or to interfere with a legitimate provincial legislative decision not to provide rights in a given area.

However, there are limits within which this approach should apply. For example, in my view,
if the provinces chose to enact human rights legislation which only prohibited discrimination on the basis of sex, and not age, this legislation could not be held to violate the
Charter
. [Emphasis added.]

It has been argued elsewhere that Justice L'Heureux-Dubé's
obiter

comments in
McKinney
have been effectively overtaken by her concurrence in the judgment of Wilson J.
in
Lavigne
, supra:
see D. Pothier, "
Charter
Challenges to Underinclusive Legislation: The Complexities of Sins of Omission" (1993) 19 Queen's L.J. 261 at 281.

[
129
]    Other cases suggest an "effects" approach. Reference has earlier been made to the Ontario Court of Appeal
decision in
Haig
, supra,
in which the law under attack was
s. 3
of the
Canadian Human Rights Act,
R.S.C. 1985, c. H-6. This provision omitted "sexual orientation" from the list of proscribed grounds of discrimination. Krever J.A. considered whether Parliament had acted in a discriminatory fashion by failing to include sexual orientation in the
Act.
At p. 8 [D/229, para. 11], he noted the appellant's argument that Parliament could have chosen not to enact a human rights Act "and, having chosen to enact one, was free to legislate in respect of some social problems and not others." At p. 9 [D/230], he concluded that, by omitting reference to homosexuals in s. 3(1) of the
Act,
homosexuals had been denied access to the ameliorating procedures of the
Act.
Thus a group that historically had been the object of discrimination on grounds analogous to those listed in
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
was withheld benefits and advantages available to other persons. At p. 10 [D/230, para. 14] he also considered the larger social, political and legal context, concluding that:

The failure to provide an avenue for redress for prejudicial treatment of homosexual members of society, and the possible inference from the omission that such treatment is acceptable,
create the effect of discrimination
offending
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.
[Emphasis added.]

[
130
]    Also relevant is
Adler
v.
Ontario

(1994),
1994 CanLII 1451 (ON CA)
,
19 O.R. (3d) 1
; leave to appeal granted, S.C.C. Bulletin 3, February 1995. In that case, parents who, because of their religious beliefs, sent their children to independent religious-based schools, attacked the constitutionality of the lack of public funding for such schools. Dubin C.J.O. rejected the claim, in part because of his conclusion that it was the religion of the claimants and not the provincial
Education Act
[R.S.O. 1990, c. E.2] that caused the appellants not to send their children to the publicly funded school system. The children had access to the public school system regardless of their religion.

[
131
]
In
Eldridge
, supra,
the plaintiffs (who were all born deaf) claimed a breach of
s. 15(1)
when funding for a medical interpreting service was ended. Citing Iacobucci J.
in
Symes
, supra,
the majority noted that
s. 15(1)
may be triggered if the
effect
of the legislation is to create a distinction resulting in discrimination against a disadvantaged group.

[
132
]
In
Symes
, supra,
at 765, Iacobucci J. had underscored the need to distinguish between "effects which are wholly caused, or are contributed to, by an impugned provision, and those social circumstances which exist independently of such a provision." The majority
in
Eldridge
, supra,
reasoned that, if the impugned legislation did not exist, both deaf and hearing people would be in the similar position of having to pay their doctors. The effect of the legislation was that, per Hollinrake J.A. at para. 35:

[T]he deaf remain responsible for the payment of translators in order to receive equivalent medical services as those with hearing, as they would be in the absence of the legislation.
This inequality exists independently of the legislation and cannot be said in any way to be an effect of the legislation
.[Emphasis added.]

[
133
]    Lambert J.A. viewed the problem from a different perspective. He asked, at para. 50, "whether the new law confers a new benefit to which the disadvantaged group do not have the same access as others outside the disadvantaged group." He concluded that translation services were integral to the provision of medical treatment, since without translation there could be no effective communication between the deaf patient and the medical practitioner. As such, there was adverse effect discrimination. While he does not frame the "distinction" issue in quite the same way as I have, his opinion seems to mean that the
failure
to extend services to deaf people could result in a distinction because of its particular effect upon that group. I acknowledge that
Adler, supra,
is somewhat different than this case because it involved the withdrawal of services that previously had been extended to the complainant group.

[
134
]
In
Symes
, supra,
Iacobucci J. rejected the
s. 15(1)
claim because, in his view, the appellant had failed to prove that impugned provisions of the
Income Tax Act
drew a distinction based upon the personal characteristic of sex. He stated at p. 766, however, that if those provisions created an adverse
effect
on women as compared with men, a distinction could have been found based upon the personal characteristic. Thus, it may be argued that he also focussed upon an "effects" approach, as did Krever J.A.
in
Haig
, supra.

[
135
]    As I have said, I prefer the third approach. The first approach is, in my view, too narrow, given the overall object of the
Charter
.
It is clear that governments cannot avoid the impact of the
Charter
through using one legislative technique rather than another. In my opinion, nor should they
necessarily
be able to avoid the
Charter
in all cases by refusing to act or by choosing to ignore legitimate problems that are presented to them. It may be that because of the close affinity between the purposes of the
Charter
and human rights laws, human rights legislation ought to be especially susceptible to this kind of analysis.

[
136
]    On the other hand, I am concerned that the second approach is unnecessarily broad. It is certainly possible to argue that, by accepting the
Charter
,
governments have committed themselves to enacting human rights laws that are in perfect harmony with the enumerated grounds of
s. 15(1)
as well as with the analogous grounds identified over time by the courts. But this case does not require me to go that far.

[
137
]    A possible implication of the fourth approach (as demonstrated by Lambert J.A.'s
dissenting judgment in
Eldridge
, supra
) may be that, having provided benefits to some victims of discrimination in a certain context, governments will be prevented from withdrawing those benefits. Especially when the benefits are financial, such a ramification could discourage governments from acting in the first place. Arguably, that result would hinder rather than promote the objects of the
Charter
.

[
138
]    For these reasons, I prefer the third approach. This requires an examination of the context of the legislation and the purpose of omission under attack. As suggested by Wilson J.
in
Lavigne
, supra,
it is necessary to examine carefully all the circumstances "to determine whether the government ha[s] significantly encouraged or supported the act which is called into question." Here, of course, that act is the refusal to extend the
IRPA
to homosexuals.

[
139
]    While I prefer the third approach, I acknowledge that the line between "purpose/context" and "effect" may not always be clear.
In
R.
v.
Big M Drug Mart Ltd.

(1985),
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
,
18 C.C.C. 385 (S.C.C.)
, discussing the
Charter
in general and not s. 15 in particular, Dickson J. observed at 414:

In my view, both purpose and effect are relevant in determining constitutionality; either an unconstitutional purpose or an unconstitutional effect can invalidate legislation. All legislation is animated by an object the Legislature intends to achieve. This object is realized through the impact produced by the operation and application of the legislation. Purpose and effect respectively, in the sense of the legislation's object and its ultimate impact, are clearly linked, if not indivisible. Intended and actual effects have often been looked to for guidance in assessing the legislation's object and thus, its validity.

Moreover, consideration of the object of legislation is vital if rights are to be fully protected. The assessment by the courts of legislative purpose focuses scrutiny upon the aims and objectives of the Legislature and ensures that they are consonant with the guarantees enshrined in the
Charter
.
The declaration that certain objects lie outside the Legislature's power checks governmental action at the first stage of unconstitutional conduct. Further, it will provide more ready and more vigorous protection of constitutional rights by obviating the individual litigant's need to prove effects violative of
Charter
rights. It will also allow courts to dispose of cases where the object is clearly improper, without inquiring into the legislation's actual impact.

[
140
]    In approaching an examination of the purpose and context of the legislation, I am mindful of basic principles that are at the root of
Charter
analyses in general and s. 15(1) analyses in particular. For example,
in
Hunter
v.
Southam,

1984 CanLII 33 (SCC)
,
[1984] 2 S.C.R. 145
at 155,
Chief Justice Dickson noted that constitutions (including the
Charter
) must "be capable of growth and development over time to meet new social, political and historical realities often unimagined by its framers," and that this is a consideration that must be borne in mind by the judiciary in interpreting constitutional provisions. It is plain that Canadian society's understanding of the discrimination suffered by homosexuals has augmented over the past years, as demonstrated (for example) by the fact that most other provincial and territorial jurisdictions in the country (all but Alberta, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and the Northwest Territories) have extended human rights protection on the ground of sexual orientation. This is a situation where those changing circumstances and values must be reflected in the interpretation of the
Charter.

[
141
]    Moreover, as underscored by McIntyre J.
in
Andrews
, supra,
a contextual approach is to be taken to
s. 15(1)
, one that considers the content and purpose of the law as well as its impact upon those to whom it applies and those whom it excludes. It was a contextual analysis to which Madam Justice Wilson alluded
in
Lavigne
, supra,
for the purpose of considering whether permissive legislation could bring the
Charter
into play.

[
142
]    In this case, a human rights law is at issue, a law that, like the
Charter
,
is dedicated to achieving equal treatment for all the citizens of Alberta. That law is under attack because it fails to extend protection to a group in society (homosexuals) that, according to at least some members of the Supreme Court of Canada, have suffered from historical disadvantage (see, for example, the judgment of Cory J. at para. 173
et seq.
and L'Heureux-Dubé J. at para. 89
in
Egan
, supra
). The evidence here establishes that they suffer discrimination in employment. Russell J. concluded at p. 6 [D/361, para. 12] that "the discrimination homosexuals suffer is so notorious" that she could take judicial notice of it.
Following
Egan
, supra,
with its conclusion that sexual orientation is an analogous ground, the appellants abandoned their attack upon her conclusion on judicial notice. Given these considerations and the context here, it is my opinion that the
failure
to extend protection to homosexuals under the
IRPA
can be seen as a form of government action that is tantamount to approving ongoing discrimination against homosexuals. Thus, in this case, legislative silence results in the drawing of a distinction.

[
143
]    Moreover, the appellants have underscored the fact that the "Alberta Legislature has repeatedly considered adding sexual orientation and had decided against it" (appellants' factum, para. 2). Russell J. found that in 1984 the Alberta Human Rights Commission recommended amending the
Act
to include sexual orientation as a prohibited ground for discrimination in employment. She also found that on several occasions between 1984 and 1991 Ministers responsible for the amendment of the
Act
indicated their intention to introduce amendments to protect sexual orientation from discrimination; letters from some government members of the Legislative Assembly, however, indicate a lack of support for such amendments. As well, I have earlier referred to the 1985 speech to the Alberta Legislature by the Minister responsible for the
IRPA.

[
144
]    From this legislative history, I think it is plain that the discrimination suffered by homosexuals in society in general and in the workplace in particular has been clearly drawn to the attention of the Legislature. The existence of that discrimination further suggests to me that there is, in some sectors of Alberta society, a hostility toward homosexuals for reasons that have nothing to do with their individual characteristics as human beings, and everything to do with presumed characteristics ascribed to them by those members of society based only upon their membership in a group that has suffered historical disadvantage. Given this context and these facts, the purpose of the Legislature's refusal to act in this situation is to reinforce stereotypical attitudes about homosexuals and their individual worth and dignity. In light of the test outlined above, this is a case where legislative silence indeed draws a distinction for the purposes of
s. 15(1)
.

[
145
]    It remains to comment briefly on why I am unable to accept the appellants' arguments on this branch of the
s. 15(1)
analysis. They have said that no distinction is drawn in this case because homosexuals are as entitled to the protection of the
IRPA
as are heterosexuals (provided, of course, that the alleged ground of discrimination falls into one of the prohibited grounds, such as age or race). Viewed one way, they have submitted that the
effect
of the
IRPA
on Vriend is the same as on other citizens of Alberta.

[
146
]    In the excerpt from
R.
v.
Swain
quoted earlier, Lamer C.J.C. said that the "distinction" inquiry should focus "on whether the law has drawn a distinction (intentionally or otherwise) between the claimant and others, based on personal characteristics."
In
Andrews
, supra,
at 299 [D/5739, para. 41746], McIntyre J. stated that the condition of equality may only be "discerned by comparison with the condition of others in the social and political setting in which the question arises." Further, "identical treatment may frequently produce serious inequality." At p. 300 [D/5739, para. 41746] he noted that a law that treats all identically could nevertheless cause inequality, "depending on differences in personal characteristics and situations." He added at p. 314 [D/5752, para. 41768] that a complainant must show that the law has a "differential impact" upon him or her.

[
147
]    In this case. the
IRPA
is facially neutral. But Vriend's situation highlights the fact that the
IRPA
is not, in reality, neutral. Vriend cannot gain access to the process of human rights enforcement for one reason: the employment discrimination he alleges results from his personal characteristic (homosexuality) and his membership in that group. It is apparent that he is being treated differently than others who claim discrimination on one of the protected grounds listed in the
IRPA,
that is, others who do not share his immutable personal characteristic of homosexuality. He is receiving treatment that is "identical," but which causes inequality because of his personal characteristic and situation.

[
148
]    To argue that the
IRPA
treats Vriend in the same way as others is to ignore the most fundamental element of this case: it is as a result of his homosexuality, an analogous ground under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
,
that he is being treated differently. This point may be put into relief through the following analogy. Imagine that the
IRPA
contained a protection for race but not for gender, and that a woman of racial minority claimed discrimination because of her gender. In such a situation it might be said that the
IRPA
drew no distinction because it treated all members of racial minorities the same. But its impact upon her would be adverse because she would be denied the
IRPA
's protection on the very ground in relation to which she claimed discrimination. This would be a situation where identical treatment would result in a distinction being drawn. For the same reason, a distinction has been drawn here.

[
149
]    To conclude this part, I note that at p. 13 [D/365, para. 53] the trial judge said "the effect of the decision to deny homosexuals recognition under the legislation is to reinforce negative stereotyping and prejudice thereby perpetuating and implicitly condoning its occurrence." In my view this was a reasonable conclusion and one that would justify dismissing the appeal, if an "effects" analysis were to be used.

B.    Denial of Equal Benefit and Protection of the Law

[
150
]    It is easy to conclude that the distinction thus drawn has resulted in the group (homosexuals) being denied equal benefit and protection of the law.
IRPA
-protected groups have the benefit of access to the machinery of the enforcement process and the ability to enforce their rights not to be discriminated against in such areas as employment. Homosexuals are denied this benefit and protection.

C.    Discrimination

[
151
]    Does the above distinction result in discrimination?
In light of
Egan
, supra,
in particular and the trilogy in general, the answer is surely yes. For notwithstanding the final result
in
Egan
,
the Supreme Court of Canada has stated clearly that "sexual orientation" is an analogous ground for the purpose of
s. 15(1)
.

[
152
]    If one were to apply the approach taken in the trilogy by McLachlin, Cory and Iacobucci JJ., it is apparent that discrimination would be found.
In
Egan
, supra,
for example, Cory J. asked whether the difference in treatment was closely related to a personal characteristic of the group to which the claimant belongs. Here, the difference in treatment results from Vriend's sexual orientation. At para. 179, Cory J. said that the existence of discrimination is determined by assessing the prejudicial effect of the distinction against
s. 15(1)
's purpose of preventing the infringement of essential human dignity. This must be looked at from the point of view of the claimant. From Vriend's perspective he is being denied the equal protection and benefit of the law
not
because of his merit or his need but purely because of his homosexuality. He was fired not because of his own abilities as a teacher but because of presumed characteristics attributed to him by virtue of his homosexuality.
In
Egan
,
Cory J. said that the denial to homosexuals of equal benefit of the law, based not on need but on sexual orientation, reinforces the stereotype that homosexuals do not form lasting relationships in the same manner as do heterosexual couples. He said that the effect of this stereotype is contrary to the purpose of
s. 15(1)
(para. 180). By analogy, denial of access to the machinery of the
IRPA
reinforces the stereotype that homosexuals are less deserving of the resulting protection and thus, to paraphrase L'Heureux-Dubé J., less worthy of value as human beings.

[
153
]    Even taking the Gonthier/La Forest JJ. approach, it is hard to see how one could fail to find discrimination here. The functional values underlying the
IRPA
must surely be found in the preamble to the
IRPA,
which refers to "the inherent dignity of all persons"; it is true that the paragraph following specifically refers to equality according to the listed protected grounds. But it is impossible to see how a statute based upon notions of the inherent dignity of all can have as a relevant legislative goal the unequal treatment of some members of society as regards employment,
on grounds that have absolutely nothing to do with their individual worth and everything to do with the fact that they belong to a group that is assumed, stereotypically, to share certain characteristics
. Thus, this is a case where, as Gonthier J. said in
Miron, supra,
the functional values underlying the omission of homosexuals are themselves discriminatory.

D.    Other Matters

[
154
]    The appellants have argued that deference should be accorded to the choice made by the Legislature not to include sexual orientation as a prohibited ground. They have said that the
Charter
should not be allowed to do through the back door what it cannot do through the front and that such will be the result if the
IRPA
has to include not only
s. 15(1)
grounds but possibly even more controversial "analogous" grounds.

[
155
]    There are a number of responses. As I have explained above, my conclusion is
not
necessarily that human rights laws must mirror perfectly the
s. 15(1)
grounds and analogous grounds, but that legislatures cannot insulate themselves from
Charter
scrutiny merely by refusing to act; whether that failure to act will breach
s. 15(1)
will depend upon the context and purpose of what they have done.

[
156
]    Courts must do the duty entrusted to them by Parliament and the legislatures and assess whether claimed
Charter
breaches have been established. This will often require the courts to second-guess legislative choices and make social policy; this is an inevitable part of the
Charter
task, especially in the context of the
s. 15(1)
guarantee of equality,
described by McIntyre J. in
Andrews
, supra,
as an "exclusive concept" that "lacks precise definition." We have been assigned the difficult job of arbitrating between legislatures and those who claim to have suffered discrimination at the hands of government. We are obliged to fulfil this obligation by applying principles developed through the case law. Once an unjustified breach of the
Charter
has been established, it is our responsibility to compel governments to fulfil their constitutional obligations.

[
157
]    In my view, the matter of legislative deference properly comes into play in the s. 1 analysis. It is trite to note that
Charter
rights are not absolute. Governments can justify
Charter
breaches through the provisions of s. 1; it is at that stage that consideration should be given to the difficult choices that legislatures have to make and to the reasons why a particular
Charter
breach may be justified.

[
158
]    Moreover, legislatures can use the "opting out" provision of the
Charter
to override the judgment of the courts. Thus the power of the courts is neither absolute nor final.

E.    Conclusion on
Section 15(1)

[
159
]    To recapitulate, it is my view that a Legislature is not immune from
s. 15(1)
scrutiny merely because it is silent or fails to act. A distinction for the purposes of
s. 15(1)
can be drawn even as a result of a legislative omission. Whether that will be the case will depend upon such factors as context and purpose.

[
160
]    In this case, I am satisfied that a distinction has been drawn between homosexuals and other victims of discrimination through the Alberta Legislature's refusal to make homosexuality a prohibited ground of discrimination under the
IRPA.
As a result, Vriend has been denied equal benefit and protection of the law. This distinction is discriminatory.

SECTION 1 OF THE CHARTER

[
161
]    Russell J. concluded that the appellants had failed to establish that the
s. 15(1)
violation was a reasonable limit that could be justified in a free and democratic society, according to the terms of
s. 1
of the
Charter
.
She
noted that
Andrews
, supra,
places the onus on the Crown to justify any infringement and that the Crown in this case had presented no rationale to show that the violation was justified. Applying
the principles in
R.
v.
Oakes
,

1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
,
[1986] 1 S.C.R. 103
,
24 C.C.C. (3d) 321
, she said the violation could not be justified.

[
162
]    No evidence was presented in this case by the Crown concerning justification under s. 1. In its factum, however, it has offered the following as possible reasons why, when the matter was debated by the Alberta Legislature in 1985 and considered at various other times, a decision was made not to add sexual orientation to the
IRPA:

”¢      The
IRPA
is inadequate to address some of the concerns expressed by the homosexual community (e.g., parental acceptance) (para. 37)

”¢      Attitudes cannot be changed by order of the Human Rights Commission (para. 37)

”¢      Codification of marginal grounds which affect few persons raises objections from larger numbers of others, adding to the number of exemptions that would have been needed to satisfy both groups (para. 41)

”¢      The purpose of the
IRPA
is not undercut by the fact that it does not include "more controversial grounds" (para. 48)

”¢      The legislation has been changed progressively as the Legislature thought the timing was right, both socially and democratically. The content and timing of incremental change should be judged by the Legislature in accordance with the consensus of Albertans as to what at a particular time constitutes social justice (para. 49)

[
163
]
In
Symes
, supra,
Iacobucci J. expressed concern about the fact that the government had failed to put forward information that was specifically related to a s. 1 analysis, but had instead chosen to rely upon general background material. He underscored at pp. 772–73 that the courts should not be left in a factual vacuum when called upon to determine a legislative objective.

[
164
]    That is precisely the situation here. We are being asked to reach conclusions based upon statements from
Hansard
and the legislative history of the
IRPA.
On its face, this material is inadequate to conduct a s. 1 analysis. In contrast to this case, in
cases such as
McKinney
and
Egan, supra,
the courts had extensive evidence [with] which to undertake a s. 1 analysis.

[
165
]    In my opinion, the paucity of the appellants' case would, of itself, support the conclusion of Russell J. that a s. 1 justification had not been established. She went on, however, to apply the
Oakes
criteria, and to reach the same conclusion. Although I agree with her analysis, I will briefly discuss these criteria, particularly taking account of some of the appellants' newer
arguments based on
Egan
, supra.

The
Oakes
tests
have been
described by Iacobucci J. in
Egan
, supra,
at para.
182
as follows:

First, the objective of the legislation must be pressing and substantial. Second, the means chosen to attain this legislative end must be reasonable and demonstrably justifiable in a free and democratic society. In order to satisfy the second requirement, three criteria must be satisfied: (1) the rights violation must be rationally connected to the aim of the legislation; (2) the impugned provision must minimally impair the
Charter
guarantee; and (3) there must be a proportionality between the effect of the measure and its objective so that the attainment of the legislative goal is not outweighed by the abridgement of the right. In all s. 1 cases the burden of proof is with the government to show on a balance of probabilities that the violation is justifiable.

I.    Is the Objective of the Legislation Pressing and Substantial?

[
166
]    The appellants have argued that "the purpose of the
IRPA
is constitutionally sound, and so the Purpose Test is met" (para. 47). While the purpose of the
IRPA
is constitutionally sound, that is not the issue. Rather, the pertinent question, per McIntyre J.
in
Andrews
, supra,
at 184 [D/5753, para. 41773], is:

[T]he first question the Court should ask must relate to the nature and the purpose of the enactment,
with a view to deciding whether the limitation represents a legitimate exercise of the legislative power for the attainment of a desirable social objective which would warrant overriding constitutionally protected rights
. [Emphasis added.]

In conformity with this
reasoning, in
Egan
, supra,
at para.
184
, Iacobucci J. considered not just the legislative objective of the
Old Age Security Act
{R.S.C. 1985, c. O-9] but, more particularly, the objective of the impugned spousal allowance.

[
167
]    Russell J. correctly applied the
Oakes
tests
in asking whether the impugned limitation (the omission of sexual orientation) was for pressing and substantial reasons. She properly concluded that this omission controverted the very purpose of the
IRPA
(recognition of the inherent dignity and equal rights of all persons) and was not "a legitimate exercise of the legislative power for the attainment of a desirable social objective which would warrant overriding constitutionally protected rights."

[
168
]    I agree with her that there is no evidence of a legislative objective of pressing and substantial concern justifying the limitation. I have already listed the justifications that can be gleaned from the appellants' factum; none are persuasive that the Crown's burden has been met.

[
169
]    For example, the fact that legislating protection from discrimination in areas such as employment would not meet all the concerns of the homosexual community (such as parental acceptance) can hardly be seen as pressing reason for not affording protection in such an important area as employment. As for the suggestion that legislation cannot change attitudes, there is no evidence to support this proposition; and even if the proposition were accepted as correct, that would not establish a pressing reason for the omission. An employer may not like the fact that discriminating against someone on a prohibited ground is illegal, but the fact that such behaviour is illegal will, at the least, ensure that the member of the disadvantaged group has a job and an opportunity to prove himself or herself on an individual basis, rather than having group characteristics ascribed to him or her.

[
170
]    Nor is the controversial nature of protection for homosexuals a pressing concern. Many other human rights protections have also been controversial in their time. Such an argument flies in the face of the purpose of the
Charter
and the
IRPA.
Presumably, it is because some sectors of society refuse equal treatment to certain disadvantaged groups that legislation such as the
IRPA
is necessary. As this Court has said in another context, "Unpopularity of
Charter
rights is not a valid factor when assessing
Charter
rights,"
Reference re Electoral Divisions Statutes Amendment Act, 1993 (Alberta)

(1995),
1994 ABCA 342 (CanLII)
,
24 Alta. L.R. (3d) 1
at 21
. To similar effect is the opinion of McLachlin J. in
R.J.R.-MacDonald Inc.
v.
Canada (Attorney General)

(1995),
1995 CanLII 64 (SCC)
,
187 N.R. 1 (S.C.C.)
. At pp. 11–12 she said that, in considering whether a
Charter
infringement is reasonable, "[t]he question is not whether the measure is popular or accords with the current public opinion polls. The question is whether it can be justified by application of the processes of reason." Here, it cannot.

II.    Is the Rights Violation Rationally Connected to the of the Legislation?

[
171
]    The appellants have argued that the rational connection test is met because the enumerated grounds in the
IRPA
are the fundamental grounds found in the
Charter
and in the human rights laws of other jurisdictions. This argument ignores the fact that sexual orientation is an analogous ground under
s. 15(1)
, has been read into the federal
Human Rights Act

in
Haig
, supra,
and is a protected ground in most other provincial and territorial human rights enactments.

[
172
]    Moreover, I accept the respondent's argument that the correct question is whether the omission of the protection can be seen to be rationally connected to the purpose of the legislation. Russell J. concluded that it was not, and I agree. The purpose of the legislation is to extend protection from discrimination to groups that have been historically disadvantaged; the omission of sexual orientation has exactly the opposite effect.

[
173
]    The appellants have argued that, according to the reasoning of Sopinka J.
in
Egan
, supra,
an "incremental approach" to legislating meets the rational connection test. But
Egan
gave rise to a different kind of problem. Specifically, it concerned the decision of the Government of Canada to extend financial benefits to some individuals and not to others. As such, there were clear financial implications resulting from the legislative choice. For example, at para. 104 Sopinka J. pointed out that "it is not realistic for the Court to assume that there are unlimited funds to address the needs of all." It is obvious that if financial benefits are extended to one group, in an era of shrinking resources other benefits may be denied to other groups. The reasons why courts should be reluctant to second-guess legislative choices when it comes to the matter of conferring financial benefits are evident.

[
174
]    I am not convinced that the same can be said for a decision not to extend human rights protection to homosexuals. There is no evidence that the extension of such protection will have any significant financial impact upon Alberta society. The human rights machinery is already in place. As Russell J. said, the extension of protection may give rise (at least in the first instance) to some new complaints. But there is nothing to suggest what the magnitude of such complaints might be, or the extent of the financial implications they might have. It is telling that the financial impact of such an inclusion is not among the justifications contained in the appellants' factum. Thus, I do not accept that Sopinka J.'s
reasoning in
Egan
, supra,
concerning "incrementalism" is applicable to this case.

III.    Does the Impugned Provision Minimally Impair the Charter Guarantee?

[
175
]
Following
Egan
, supra,
the appellants have further relied upon the reasoning of Sopinka J. to the effect that courts should not second-guess legislative decisions which require governments to mediate between the socio-economic interests of competing groups. In my view, the analogy is again inapt. There is nothing to suggest that a prohibition against discrimination against homosexuals in relation to a matter such as employment will disadvantage other groups (in the way that, as I have discussed above, payments to one group will almost inevitably mean a lack of payments to other groups). Indeed, the contrary is more likely the case. Homosexuals, like other disadvantaged members of society, have skills and talents to contribute. Vriend, for example, received positive evaluations for his teaching, before he was fired due to his homosexuality. Society will be the poorer if homosexuals are not given the even-handed opportunity to make those contributions.

[
176
]    The exclusion of homosexuals from protection under the
IRPA
is total, so there is a total impairment of the
Charter
guarantee of equality. There is no evidence that the Alberta Legislature carefully balanced competing interests, for example, concluding that there were sound reasons to afford protection to homosexuals in regard to housing but not in regard to employment.

IV.    Is there Proportionality Between the Effect of the Measure and its Objective Such that the Attainment of the Legislative Goal is not Outweighed by the Abridgement of the Right?

[
177
]    Noting that there had been in this case no rationale put forward to show that the Legislature had been faced with "a choice of conflicting scientific evidence and differing demands on scarce resources," Russell J. concluded that there was not proportionality between the attainment of any legislative goal and the abridgement of Vriend's right to equality. I agree. There has been a total denial of his rights and a total failure to justify that denial.

[
178
]    The appellants have also relied upon the decision of Sopinka J.
in
Egan
, supra,
as to this branch of the
Oakes
tests.
Again, the two cases are not comparable. The following extract from para. 111 of his decision underscores that human rights legislation raises different problems of legislative choice than does legislation relating to the provision of social benefits:

Moreover, human rights legislation operates in the field of employment, housing, use of public facilities and the like. This can hardly be equated with the problems faced by the federal government which must assess the impact of extending the benefits contained in some fifty federal statutes.

REMEDY

[
179
]    Russell J. considered
the principles of
Osborne
v.
Canada (Treasury Board)

(1991),
125 N.R. 214 (S.C.C.)
and
Schachter
v.
The Queen

(1992),
1992 CanLII 74 (SCC)
,
93 D.L.R. (4th) 1
. She concluded that the appropriate remedy was to read the words "sexual orientation" into the impugned provisions, without a delay period. She rejected the notion of striking down the legislation, reasoning at p. 18 [D/368, para. 77] that

”¦ because the objective of human rights legislation is consistent with the purposes of the
Charter
,
it is safe to assume that the Legislature would have preferred an
Act
with sexual orientation included than no
Act
at all. That assumption is supported by the preamble to the
Act
which recognizes the inherent dignity and the equal and inalienable rights of all persons.

[
180
]    In the result, she declared that ss. 2(1), 3, 4, 7(1), 8(1) and 10 of the
IRPA
are inconsistent with
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
and that the sections be [D/369, para. 84] "interpreted, applied and administered as though they contained the words ”˜sexual orientation.'" Those sections are found in Appendix A [not published here].

[
181
]    Before proceeding, I wish to note that there was no argument before us as to the appropriateness of fashioning a remedy
vis-à-vis
all six impugned sections, even though the evidence before the Court, as it concerned Vriend, related only to discrimination in employment. Indeed, it is evident from the decision of Russell J. that she heard preliminary argument about whether s. 10 could also be considered in the application, it having been omitted in the notice of motion by oversight. She concluded that s. 10 could be considered, because the applicants had established standing to challenge it (based upon the "public interest principles"
outlined by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Canadian Council of Churches
v.
Canada

(1992),
1992 CanLII 116 (SCC)
,
88 D.L.R. (4th) 193
. She stated that the only way to challenge s. 10 would be to bring an application similar to this one before the Court and that it would be unreasonable to require another comparable application concerning what is essentially the same issue.

[
182
]    I have given this matter considerable thought since oral argument and since receiving supplementary factums dealing with
Egan, supra.
I appreciate that the issues concerning all six sections may be very similar.

[
183
]    On the other hand I am mindful of the admonition that
Charter
cases are not to be considered in a factual vacuum,
MacKay
v.
Manitoba

(1989),
1989 CanLII 26 (SCC)
,
61 D.L.R. (4th) 385
,
[1989] 6 W.W.R. 351 (S.C.C.)
. Moreover, it is of some significance that these six sections do not all prohibit discrimination on the same grounds. Specifically, ss. 7, 8 and 10 contain reference to marital status as a prohibited ground, which ss. 2, 3 and 4 do not. There are other differences. Section 7, which concerns employment practices, contains an escape clause in subsection (3), as to
bona fide
occupational requirements (BFORs). In addition, subsection (2) states that the prohibition in (1) as to discrimination in employment "as it relates to age and marital status does not affect the operation of any
bona fide
retirement or pension plan or the terms or conditions of any
bona fide
group or employee insurance plan." Section 8, which concerns applications and advertisements regarding employment, also contains a limitation in subsection (2) as to BFORs. These differences render even more problematic the task of selecting an appropriate remedy.

[
184
]    I have concluded that, whatever the remedy, it should be limited to the evidence in this case, namely, that Vriend was fired from his job because of his homosexuality. He was not discriminated against by virtue of a public notice (s. 2); denied public accommodation (s. 3); or denied a tenancy (s. 4). Nor, it must be acknowledged, was he discriminated against in an employment notice (s. 8) or denied membership in a union (s. 10). However, in my opinion the latter two provisions are sufficiently related to the facts before the Court to justify including them in the remedy. It would be odd if one could not be discriminated against as to employment, but could be discriminated against as regards employment notices and membership in organizations related to employment.

[
185
]    In thus limiting my discussion of a remedy, I should
not
be taken to say that the outlined principles would not also apply to discrimination pursuant to the other three sections. On the contrary, it is my view that the same principles would apply. However, the facts giving rise to a case under those other sections are not before the Court. Accordingly, in what follows I will limit my discussion to ss. 7, 8 and 10 (while pointing out that the arguments of the parties were not so limited).

[
186
]
Schachter, supra,
concerned whether the
Unemployment Insurance Act
fell afoul of the
Charter
because it granted parental leave to adoptive parents but not to natural parents. Having found that the legislation breached s. 15 by virtue of its under-inclusivity, the trial judge declared that other persons in similar circumstances were entitled to the same parental leave benefits, until such time as Parliament amended the
Act
so as to meet the requirements of s. 15. Before the Court of Appeal, the parties conceded the s. 15 violation and the matter proceeded on the question of remedy. By the time the appeal was argued, Parliament had amended the offending legislation so as to extend parental benefits to natural parents on the same basis as to adoptive parents; however, Parliament had reduced the period of parental leave from fifteen to ten weeks.

[
187
]    For the majority, Chief Justice Lamer reviewed the possible ways of remedying a
Charter
breach. He said these included striking down to the extent of the
Charter
inconsistency, striking down with a temporary suspension of invalidity, reading down or reading in. In selecting a remedy, he stated that reference should be made to the nature of the
Charter
violation and the context of the specific legislation. Underlying principles are respect for the role of the legislature and respect for the purposes of the
Charter.
He underscored at p. 25 that "there is no easy formula by which a court may decide whether severance or reading in is appropriate in a given case."

[
188
]    Per Lamer C.J.C., the first step in choosing a remedy is defining the extent of the inconsistency. Here, it is the failure to extend to homosexuals the protection of the
IRPA
in relation to discrimination in employment and related matters.

[
189
]    A number of cases concerning the exclusion of homosexuals from legislative benefits have given rise to remedy issues.
In
Haig
, supra,
which is closest to the situation here, Krever J.A. determined that it was appropriate to read the words "sexual orientation" into s. 3 of the federal human rights legislation, which set out prohibited grounds of discrimination. That legislation was structured differently than the
IRPA.
The offending provision (containing the prohibited grounds of discrimination) was so pivotal that, according to Krever J.A., to sever it would be to strike down the whole
Act.
Striking down alone would not give the applicants access to the remedial legislation that they required and it would deny access to large numbers of other people. Thus he concluded that reading in was appropriate.

[
190
]
Haig, supra,
also differs from this case because there was evidence of a governmental commitment to add sexual orientation to s. 3. Here, the very opposite is true.

[
191
]    In
Knodel
v.
B.C.
(1991), 91 C.L.L.C. para. 17,023 (B.C.S.C.), Rowles J. granted a declaration that the definition of "spouse" in regulations under the
Medical Services Act
included same sex couples, with the result that such couples were entitled to medical coverage on the same basis as opposite sex couples. Like
Haig, supra,
the structure of the statute was more simple than the
IRPA.

[
192
]
In
Egan
, supra,
only Iacobucci J. discussed a remedy. As
in
Knodel
, supra,
the definition of "spouse" made specific reference to opposite sex couples. Iacobucci J. was prepared to read out the words "of the opposite sex" and read in the words "or as an analogous relationship."

[
193
]    He reasoned that the problem with the legislation was its under-inclusiveness, which emanated from an exclusionary distinction based on the irrelevant ground of sexual orientation. He said it would be absurd to invalidate the spousal allowance. The offending portion of the statute (being the opposite sex requirement) could be defined in a limited manner and so only that limited portion should be declared inoperative.

[
194
]    "Remedial precision," according to Iacobucci J., existed because the constitutional wrong could be corrected with a handful of words. Reading same-sex couples into the scheme would not be at odds with the goal of a spousal allowance but would promote the attainment of legislative goals. It was likely that the legislature would have passed the legislation with the inclusion, if the alternative was to not have the legislation at all. Budgetary issues were not a factor because the evidence about the cost of extending the benefits was equivocal.

[
195
]    Iacobucci J. was prepared to suspend the remedy for a year because of his view that, due to public policy concerns [
sic
]. He said Parliament ought to be given the latitude to devise its own approach and to co-ordinate its approach with the provinces.

[
196
]    Reading in was also the remedy
in
Tighe (Guardian ad litem)
v.
McGillivray Estate

(1994),
1994 NSCA 28 (CanLII)
,
112 D.L.R. (4th) 201 (N.S.C.A.)
. There the problem was that a section of the
Intestate Succession Act
discriminated against illegitimate children by disallowing them from inheriting from their fathers' estates. Again, this was easily remedied by adding the words "or father" into the provision.

[
197
]
Schachter, supra,
makes it plain that, in the right circumstances, reading in can be a remedy. It is to be used only in the clearest of cases, namely, (1) where the legislative objective is obvious and reading in would further that objective or interfere less with the objective than would striking down; (2) the choice of means used by the Legislature to further the objective is not so unequivocal that reading in would unacceptably intrude into the domain of the Legislature; and (3) reading in would not intrude substantially into the Legislature's budgetary decisions (p. 28). At p. 18 it was pointed out that reading in should
not
be used when the question of how to amend the statute to comply with the
Constitution
cannot be answered with sufficient precision, for it is the Legislature and not the courts who should fill in the necessary details. Only after the remedy has been chosen should consideration be given to whether the declaration of invalidity ought to be temporarily suspended (p. 28).

[
198
]
In
Schachter
, supra,
Chief Justice Lamer, for the majority, concluded that the appropriate remedy would have been to declare the offending provision invalid but to suspend the declaration of invalidity so as to allow Parliament the opportunity to amend the legislation. Among his reasons for this conclusion [was] that, since the legislation extended a benefit, it would be wrong to strike it down immediately since that would deprive others of benefits without providing any relief to the respondents. He said that, while it was easy to discern the overall purpose of the legislation, the purpose of the particular provision at issue was less clear. Without this, he considered it imprudent to read in the excluded group.

[
199
]    There are many arguments here for reading in. The
IRPA
's overall objectives are in harmony with the objectives of the
Charter
;
thus, striking down the offending portions of the
Act
would be contrary to the objectives of the
Charter.
Reading in is required in order to relieve the disadvantaged position of the excluded group, homosexuals. The resulting intrusion into budgetary matters, if any, would be slight. The group to be added is considerably smaller than the group that would be affected were the legislation struck down in its entirety.

[
200
]    On the other hand, I am concerned about whether, in this case, reading in can be accomplished with adequate precision. One problem is whether it is necessary to have a definition of "sexual orientation." It is true that neither Krever J.A.
in
Haig
, supra,
nor Iacobucci J.
in
Egan
, supra,
expressed concern about this. It is also true, as noted by Russell J., that many other provincial human rights laws have included the term "sexual orientation" without defining it. However, as I have said, the statutory contexts of
Egan
and
Knodel, supra,
were such that the reading in clearly addressed the situation of homosexual couples. Thus there was no need to use the arguably broader term "sexual orientation." Similarly,
in
Tighe
, supra,
the reading in could be accomplished with simplicity. For reasons outlined above, that is not so in this case.

[
201
]    Also troublesome is the possible impact of the proposed reading in upon the operation of s. 7(2) of the
IRPA.
As noted earlier, it states that s. 7(1), as regards age and marital status, "does not affect the operation of any
bona fide
retirement or pension plan or the terms or conditions of any
bona fide
group or employee insurance plan." The remedy granted by Russell J. appears not to include "sexual orientation" in the exclusion found in subsection (2). We heard no argument on this point and there is no evidence before the Court to explain the rationale behind this provision. It seems to me that in extending the protection of the
IRPA
to homosexuals, some thought would have to be given to whether or not that group would be included or excluded from subsection (2), and, if they were to be excluded, whether the exclusion could be justified under s. 1. This is something the Court is in no position to do. Given this difficulty, I am concerned that the reading in remedy would engage the Court in the kind of "filling in of details" against which Lamer C.J.C. cautions
in
Schachter
, supra.

[
202
]    Having concluded that this is not a sufficiently clear case for reading in, the remaining option is to declare invalid the offending sections to the extent of their inconsistency with the
Charter
,
namely, to the extent that they do not provide protection to homosexuals.

[
203
]    This leaves the question of whether the declaration of invalidity ought to be delayed.
In
Schachter
, supra,
Chief Justice Lamer separately considered the circumstances under which it would be appropriate to employ a temporary suspension of a declaration of invalidity. At p. 26 he stated:

A delayed declaration is a serious matter from the point of view of the enforcement of the
Charter
.

A delayed declaration allows a state of affairs which has been found to violate standards embodied in the
Charter
to persist for a time despite the violation
. There may be good pragmatic reasons to allow this in particular cases. However,
reading in is much preferable where it is appropriate, since it immediately reconciles the legislation in question with the requirements of the
Charter
. [Emphasis added.]

[
204
]    In this case, an immediate declaration of invalidity would remove the
IRPA
's protection from everyone, without granting any relief to homosexuals. This result would be less in harmony with the
Charter
's objectives than would a temporary suspension of the declaration of invalidity. On the other hand, a temporary suspension will allow the Legislature a period of time in which to conform with the
Charter
.

[
205
]    In the result, I would vary the judgment of Russell J. as follows. I would declare ss. 7(1), 8(1) and 10 of the
IRPA
to be of no force and effect to the extent that they fail to extend the protection to homosexuals. I would suspend this declaration of invalidity for a period of one year to allow the Alberta Legislature time to bring the
IRPA
into line with the
Charter
.
